articles.title: Watch: Inside French drug gangs recruiting children to kill
articles.summary: "It destroys people, but we all make our own choices" - Marseille drug-gang members spoke to the BBC.
articles.body:
A BBC investigation has found one of Europe's most powerful drug gangs in France is recruiting teenage children from across the country to commit kidnap and murder.

Known as the "DZ Mafia", the gang won a bloody turf war against a rival group in Marseille during 2023, and is now recruiting from further afield.

One member who is in prison awaiting trial after being implicated in several murders told the BBC he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad.

He agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".

"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."

When challenged over whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality, he says he feels "guilty in-part" but claims to have no regrets.

Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".

The BBC's Paris Correspondent, James Waterhouse, reports from Marseille.

articles.title: Pope Leo urges President Milei, a Trump ally, to ‘safeguard democracy’ on arrival in Argentina
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV has called on Argentine President Javier Milei and the country’s political leaders to “safeguard democracy” and demonstrate a “careful use of words” during his first speech in Buenos Aires.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV called on Argentine President Javier Milei and the country’s political leaders to “safeguard democracy” and demonstrate a “careful use of words” during his first speech in Buenos Aires. The American pope arrived in Argentina on Sunday, embarking on a trip that his predecessor, the first Argentine pope, was never able to make. Leo’s highly anticipated papal visit to Argentina began with a private meeting with President Milei shortly after the pope landed. Milei has received strong backing from US President Donald Trump, with whom Leo, first American pontiff, has publicly disagreed, particularly on the treatment of migrants and the war in Iran. The pope’s visit comes at a time when Milei’s “chainsaw” austerity measures have led to welfare spending cuts. Milei has also equated state-led social justice programs with communism and has also been accused of undermining democracy through attacks on the press and divisive rhetoric. He has also struggled to secure bipartisan agreements. “Democracy, then, is also a part of Argentina’s heritage that needs to be safeguarded,” the pope said at a meeting with politicians, members of civic society and the diplomatic corps at the Palacio Libertad. “Democracy is also strengthened by the daily conduct of public life: through willingness to listen, through careful use of words, through the patient search for agreement, and through the ability to see those who think differently as fellow citizens with whom we share a common future.” The Chicago-born pontiff, who recently cast a mail-in ballot during the US mid-term elections, talked about the importance of the “freedom to elect one’s own leaders through the ballot box.” He urged leaders to recognize the limits of their power, and said that democracy is protected by “confidence in the law”, the ability to freely express convictions and for institutions to serve all parties. “Authority is most authentic when it is exercised as service, when it looks beyond the immediate, and when it uses its power to promote the welfare of all,” the pope said. An eruption of applause from the audience forced him to repeat his next line: “Those who exercise authority have a duty to act with prudence, to acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them.” Leo’s November 8-11 trip is the first papal visit to Argentina in almost four decades and it comes with the added dimension that Pope Francis did not make a return trip home during his 12-year-papacy. Millions are expected to attend the various services and events while the pope is in the country. A mass held Monday drew a crowd of roughly 2.5 million people, according to official estimates, making it the largest event Pope Leo has held in his papacy thus far. It also surpasses the numbers that turned out in the same spot for Pope John Paul II in 1982. One Argentine woman, Milagros, told CNN that Francis had baptized her before he became pope. She said Leo’s papacy had brought her back into the fold, and she now attends more religious services. “The pope’s message reached me late, but it reached me,” Milagros said. After mass, Leo visited with five people who had suffered abuse by Catholic clergy or within church organizations. A Vatican press release said the pope “greeted them together, imparted his blessing upon them, and expressed his gratitude for the meeting and for their witness of faith.” Francis’ decision not to visit Argentina was something even his closest friends were unable to explain. Some have suggested the late pope’s reluctance to visit was linked to Argentina’s polarized political culture, with Francis wary that his presence in the country could be weaponized. The Argentine pope had a strong emphasis on the church helping the most marginalized in society. Francis lamented Argentina’s economic decline which he blamed on decades of bad governance. He contrasted the roughly 5% inflation rate he recalled from his youth with the soaring inflation and high poverty rates of recent years. In his speech, Leo cited Argentina’s “abundance of human resources” but called for its “wealth bear fruit for the benefit of all and warned that corruption undermines trust in institutions. Before his election as pope in 2013, Francis served as archbishop of Buenos Aires, where he spoke out on social justice and was unafraid to criticize political leaders. Leo’s visit, the second leg of his 12-day tour of South America, will underline the ways he continues the reforms of his predecessor, but with his own distinctive style. Pope Leo, in contrast, has made the church’s social teaching and concern for the marginalized a central concern of his papacy. His itinerary in Argentina includes a visit to a federal prison in Buenos Aires and a stop at a care center for people with intellectual and physical disabilities in Claypole which has been affected by the Milei cuts. During his presidential campaign and in the years leading up to it, Milei repeatedly insulted Francis, calling him an “imbecile” for defending social justice, “the representative of the evil one on earth” and a “sh*t of a pope.” Milei later apologized for these remarks and called Francis “the most important Argentine in history” following the pontiff’s death in April 2025, repeating the compliment in his remarks on Sunday. Milei and Francis met in the Vatican in February 2024, with the pope joking with the president: “you cut your hair!” — a reference to the unruly hairstyle which earned Milei the nickname “The Wig.” Milei replied that he had “tidied it up.” Leo and Milei previously met at the Vatican in June 2025. After meeting Milei in the Casa Rosada on his arrival in Buenos Aires, the pope was presented with the keys to the city of the Argentine capital by the mayor, Jorge Macri.

articles.title: Feirão de Negociação de Dívidas do Procon Facape em Petrolina | G1
articles.standfirst: Atendimento presencial segue até a quinta-feira (12); não é preciso se inscrever. Interessados devem levar documentos pessoais e comprovantes dos débitos.
articles.summary: O Feirão de Negociação de Dívidas em Petrolina oferece condições especiais para quitar débitos com bancos e a Compesa na sede do Procon Facape até quinta-feira.
articles.body:
Faculdade de Petrolina (Facape) — Foto: Ascom / Facape

O Procon da Faculdade de Petrolina ( Facape ), no Sertão de Pernambuco, realiza, a partir desta terça-feira (10) até quinta-feira (12), mais uma edição do Feirão de Negociação de Dívidas. O atendimento será realizado na sede do Procon Facape, das 8h às 11h e das 13h às 16h.

O objetivo do feirão é facilitar a regularização de pendências financeiras com condições facilitadas de pagamento. Estão confirmadas as participações de bancos, financeiras, administradoras de cartões de crédito, empresas de telefonia e da Companhia Pernambucana de Saneamento (Compesa).

Não é necessário fazer inscrição prévia. Os interessados devem comparecer ao local levando documentos pessoais e contas ou comprovantes das dívidas que desejam negociar.

articles.title: Apreensão de drogas em Barra Mansa: BAC usa cães em ação no Paraíso | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a polícia, cães farejadores ajudaram nas buscas no Paraíso.
articles.summary: Apreensão de drogas em Barra Mansa mobilizou o Batalhão de Ações com Cães, que localizou entorpecentes e rádio comunicadores em um prédio no bairro Paraíso.
articles.body:
BAC apreende drogas e materiais usados no tráfico em Barra Mansa — Foto: Divulgação/PMERJ.

O Batalhão de Ações com Cães apreendeu nesta segunda-feira (9) 2 kg de drogas durante uma ação no bairro Paraíso, em Barra Mansa (RJ).

Segundo a PM, policiais da 3ª Companhia do Batalhão de Ações com Cães (BAC) realizavam patrulhamento na comunidade com o auxílio das cadelas farejadoras Electra e Zara para realizar buscas na região.

Durante a ação os animais indicaram a presença de drogas no basculante de um apartamento. Os agentes fizeram buscas no bloco e encontraram uma mochila com mais drogas no sótão do prédio.

Ao todo foram apreendidos 87 trouxinhas de maconha, 27 porções de haxixe, 122 pedras de crack, 145 pinos de cocaína, 300 gramas de cocaína, 11 frasco de loló, um carregador de pistola calibre 45, duas bases de rádio comunicador e uma balança de precisão.

Até o momento ninguém foi preso durante a ocorrência. O material foi encaminhado para a delegacia de Barra Mansa, onde o caso foi registrado.

articles.title: Leão XIV acolhe pessoas com deficiência na Argentina: "não são peso" | G1
articles.standfirst: Pontífice visitou um centro de acolhimento para pessoas com deficiência e vulnerabilidade nesta segunda-feira (9) na Argentina. É a primeira visita de um papa ao país desde João Paulo II, em 1987.
articles.summary: Papa Leão XIV inicia visita histórica à Argentina com apelo à inclusão de pessoas com deficiência e críticas indiretas à agenda social do governo de Javier Milei.
articles.body:
Papa Leão XIV visita a Argentina — Foto: Reuters

O papa Leão XIV visitou nesta segunda-feira (9) um centro de atendimento a pessoas com deficiência em Buenos Aires, Argentina. Em discurso, ele ressaltou a importância da inclusão de pessoas com deficiência e em situação de vulnerabilidade.

"O progresso de uma nação também se mede pela acolhida que é capaz de oferecer a todas as pessoas com deficiência e necessidades especiais", disse o pontífice em seu discurso no Cottolengo Don Orione em Claypole, na zona sul de Buenos Aires.

"Gostaria de afirmar hoje que suas vidas não são um peso para a sociedade. São uma bênção, porque vocês podem nos ajudar a não esquecer qual é o fundamento da dignidade de cada ser humano e o que realmente importa na vida", afirmou Leão XIV.

A fala de Leão XIV acontece em meio a discordâncias do pontífice com Javier Milei, presidente da Argentina. Justiça social e combate à pobreza estão entre os pontos que separam o presidente argentino do maior líder da Igreja Católica.

Nas agendas na América do Sul, o pontífice tem reforçado críticas a medidas como o ajuste fiscal e a agenda social do governo argentino, que tem acentuado a pobreza extrema no país .

"Neste momento tão particular, gostaria de compartilhar com todos vocês meu desejo para este país: que a Argentina seja capaz de realizar grandes obras de caridade, como vemos aqui, onde o amor de Cristo triunfe sobre o individualismo e a exclusão", disse Leão XIV nesta segunda.

No último domingo, ao chegar na Argentina, o pontífice já havia feito um chamado direto a Milei , em que pediu que o líder argentino preserve a democracia e reconheça os limites do poder.

A agenda faz parte da visita do pontífice pela América do Sul, a primeira desde que assumiu o papado, em maio de 2025. Leão XIV dedicou a visita ao papa Francisco, nascido na Argentina e que nunca visitou o país natal enquanto liderou a Igreja Católica.

Esta é a primeira visita de um papa ao país desde João Paulo II, em 1987.

Missa campal pode atrair mais de um milhão e meio de pessoas

Nesta segunda-feira, Leão XIV participará ainda de uma missa campal que promete atrair pelo menos 1,5 milhão de pessoas no bairro de Palermo, em Buenos Aires.

Nas primeiras horas da manhã desta segunda, multidões já se reuniam na Avenida do Libertador, onde acontecerá a missa.

A viagem de 12 dias pela América Latina terminará no dia 17 de novembro, quando o pontífice deixará o Peru, país em que residiu por cerca de 20 anos e onde se tornou cardeal.

Imagens aéreas mostram pessoas reunidas perto do Monumento aos Espanhóis, em Buenos Aires, antes da missa que o papa Leão XIII deverá conceder durante sua viagem de 12 dias à América do Sul, na primeira visita papal à Argentina desde 1987. — Foto: Reuters

articles.title: Enem Matemática MMC: Professor usa exemplo de ônibus em dica | G1
articles.standfirst: Quadro da TV Sergipe traz orientações práticas sobre simultaneidade e mínimo múltiplo comum para ajudar os estudantes na reta final de estudos.
articles.summary: Com foco no Enem, professor de Sergipe ensina técnica rápida para resolver MMC e identificar problemas de simultaneidade usando exemplos de transporte público.
articles.body:
A preparação para o Exame Nacional do Enem ganha mais um reforço com o quadro Conexão Enem. Nesta edição, gravada às margens do Rio Sergipe, o foco é a disciplina de matemática, abordando um tema recorrente nas provas: o Mínimo Múltiplo Comum (MMC).

Para ilustrar como o conceito é cobrado no exame, o professor Arilson utilizou o exemplo prático de ônibus com destinos diferentes que partem do mesmo terminal. Suponha que um veículo faça o percurso em 30 minutos e o outro, em 40 minutos. Para descobrir em quanto tempo eles passarão juntos novamente no ponto de partida, utiliza-se o cálculo do MMC.

Enem em Sergipe: professor usa exemplo de transporte público para explicar cálculo de MMC em dica de matemática — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Sergipe

Durante a explicação, o ´professor demonstrou uma técnica rápida para resolver a operação de cabeça:

Compara-se o maior número (40) com o menor (30). Como 40 não é divisível por 30, soma-se mais 40, obtendo 80 (também não divisível).

Somando mais 40, chega-se a 120, valor que é divisível por 30.

Portanto, o intervalo de tempo em que ambos passarão juntos novamente no ponto é de 120 minutos (duas horas).

O professor destacou que os estudantes devem redobrar a atenção quando identificarem termos como "juntos" e "juntos novamente" nos enunciados das questões. Esses indícios apontam que se trata de um problema de simultaneidade, cuja resolução correta passa pelo cálculo do MMC.

articles.title: Trump defende chefe do Pentágono após pedido de impeachment: 'Venceu duas guerras' | G1
articles.standfirst: Trump afirmou que Hegseth é alvo de críticas apesar dos resultados das operações militares americanas. Deputado republicano Thomas Massie apresentou pedido de impeachment em meio à pressão pela condução da guerra contra o Irã e seus impactos econômicos.
articles.summary: Trump afirmou que Hegseth é alvo de críticas apesar dos resultados das operações militares americanas.
articles.body:
O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump , saiu em defesa do secretário de Guerra, Pete Hegseth, nesta segunda-feira (9), em meio à pressão por seu impeachment.

Em entrevista à agência de notícias Reuters, Trump minimizou as críticas contra que o chefe do Pentágono e exaltou resultados de operações militares americanas: "Ele é culpado de duas coisas, basicamente: vencer duas guerras".

👉 Trump se referiu tanto à guerra contra o Irã, que está em um impasse, quanto à operação militar dos EUA na Venezuela que resultou na captura de Nicolás Maduro.

"E quanto a pedir o impeachment dos responsáveis pelo Vietnã, Afeganistão, Iraque e tudo mais, onde lutamos por uma eternidade e nada aconteceu?", afirmou Trump.

O pedido de impeachment foi apresentado mais cedo pelo deputado republicano Thomas Massie, representante do estado de Kentucky, na Câmara dos Estados Unidos.

A iniciativa ocorre em meio ao aumento das críticas à condução da guerra contra o Irã e aos impactos econômicos do conflito, que contribuíram para as derrotas do Partido Republicano nas eleições de meio de mandato.

Com o resultado, a legenda perdeu o controle do Congresso.

No domingo (8), Trump já havia defendido o secretário e questionado a possibilidade de seu afastamento. "Acredito que salvamos o Oriente Médio e Israel juntos. É muito difícil dizer que alguém que fez isso deve sofrer impeachment", afirmou o presidente.

Hegseth também minimizou a ameaça de afastamento. Nesta segunda-feira, após discursar na Escola de Guerra Naval dos Estados Unidos, em Rhode Island, ele classificou as críticas como motivadas por interesses políticos e disse não estar preocupado com a pressão.

"Minha equipe não está preocupada com o barulho — foi o que também disse às tropas: não se preocupem com o barulho", declarou.

O secretário de Estado americano, Marco Rubio, também manifestou apoio a Hegseth nesta segunda-feira. Durante uma conversa com jornalistas em Paris, na França, após uma reunião de chanceleres do G7, Rubio considerou injusto o pedido de impeachment .

"Acho que é injusto. Acho que Pete fez um bom trabalho, de verdade", afirmou.

Rubio também elogiou a atuação militar americana contra o Irã e disse que as forças iranianas sofreram danos significativos. Sobre a operação para capturar o ex-presidente venezuelano Nicolás Maduro, afirmou que a ação foi executada de maneira impecável.

O secretário reconheceu, porém, que há divergências políticas sobre a atuação de Hegseth.

"Alguém precisava enfrentar a busca do regime iraniano por uma arma nuclear. A escolha era não agir e torcer para que o problema desaparecesse ou tomar uma decisão ousada", afirmou.

O Irã sustenta que seu programa nuclear tem fins pacíficos. Segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia Atômica (AIEA), o país possui 440,9 quilos de urânio enriquecido a até 60% de pureza . O nível está próximo dos 90% , percentual geralmente necessário para a produção de armas nucleares.

Hegseth afirmou que o Irã está "devastado" pela ofensiva americana.

A declaração ocorre, porém, enquanto continuam os ataques iranianos contra bases militares utilizadas pelos Estados Unidos no Oriente Médio e embarcações comerciais no Estreito de Ormuz .

As ofensivas provocaram bilhões de dólares em prejuízos às instalações militares americanas. Além disso, as interrupções no tráfego marítimo pelo Estreito de Ormuz contribuíram para a alta dos preços da energia .

Antes da guerra, a passagem concentrava cerca de um quinto do petróleo comercializado no mundo.

O aumento dos custos de energia afetou o orçamento das famílias americanas e se tornou um dos fatores de insatisfação dos eleitores com o governo Trump.

Uma pesquisa da Associated Press indicou que cerca de seis em cada dez eleitores americanos consideraram errada a decisão dos Estados Unidos de realizar operações militares contra o Irã. O levantamento ouviu mais de 100 mil eleitores.

Questionado sobre as críticas do vice-presidente JD Vance, que atribuiu à guerra parte das derrotas republicanas nas eleições de meio de mandato, Hegseth afirmou concordar com Trump, que disse que tomaria a mesma decisão novamente.

O secretário também repetiu uma declaração feita por Rubio no domingo: "Não precisa necessariamente ser popular, mas pode ser necessário".

O deputado americano Thomas Massie (republicano do Kentucky) concede entrevista coletiva sobre sua proposta de impeachment do secretário de Defesa, Pete Hegseth, no Capitólio, em Washington, nos Estados Unidos, em 9 de novembro de 2026. — Foto: Reuters/Evelyn Hockstein

articles.title: Four killed in Gaza after embankment collapses onto tents, health ministry says
articles.summary: Three children are among those killed in the incident that came a day after heavy rain reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents across Gaza.
articles.body:
Three children and one woman were killed when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents in central Gaza following heavy rain, the Hamas-run health ministry says.

Five injured people were also reportedly rescued after the incident on Sunday night at a camp for displaced families south of Deir al-Balah.

Videos showed men using phone torches to search for survivors beneath boulders, sand and collapsed tents.

The Civil Defence service, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry, said the "humanitarian tragedy" should prompt urgent action by international organisations to provide safe shelters for displaced people and move tents away from sandy areas, slopes and locations at risk of collapse.

Torrential rain on Saturday reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents across Gaza, leaving many Palestinians without a dry place to sleep.

The Civil Defence said water levels reached up to 1.5m (4.9ft) in some places and that its first responders were able to respond to only 10% of the 2,100 distress calls they received.

"Protecting the lives of displaced people is an urgent humanitarian responsibility. Their tents must not become death traps beneath sand and rainwater," it warned.

Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza

Funding shortages force World Food Programme to cut Gaza aid

Eight children among 21 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses, rescuers say

The Civil Defence initially reported on Sunday that three children and two women were killed when the sand embankment collapsed. But the health ministry said on Monday morning that only one woman was among the dead.

She was identified as Tahrir Nabhan, while the children were named as Mariam Nabhan and her brother Salah, and Habiba al-Zein.

Mustafa al-Masri told the BBC that he and other rescuers had used their bare hands to dig the victims and survivors out of the sand and rubble.

"It was extremely difficult. This mound was huge and wide. It collapsed onto the tent, and we didn't know what to do," he said.

"When we got here, we, along with the young men from the camp, pulled them out with our own hands. We pulled out the children and the woman."

"Their father arrived shouting, 'My children, my children, my children, my children.' We pulled his children out, put them in the ambulance, and took them to the hospital."

Masri added that he had been displaced from the northern town of Beit Hanoun but had stayed in central Gaza because there was "nowhere for me to return to".

"We went out looking around, searching through the open areas and hills, but I couldn't find any place other than this area that felt suitable for me."

The International Organization for Migration's regional crisis co-ordinator, Karl Baker, told the BBC from Gaza that the territory's 2.1 million population was confined to only 30% of its total area and that many people were "unfortunately living in areas which would not be normal if we were not in this time of conflict".

He said the UN agency and its partners were trying to make sure there were enough tents and tarpaulins, as well as improved drainage in camps, to help them get through the winter.

However, he warned that aid currently getting into Gaza was not sufficient to meet the demands of the population, describing it as "the very smallest of Band-Aids [plasters]".

"We need more support, in-kind donations. We need funding in order to help the communities to help themselves," he said. "We need a lot more to happen."

UN agencies have called on Israeli authorities to allow in the specialist equipment and materials required to improve living conditions for displaced families.

Cogat, the Israeli military body tasked with co-ordinating deliveries, said on Sunday that more than 91,000 tents, 12 vacuum trucks for waste removal, and fuel and engine oil for pumping facilities have been delivered since the start of the "Gaza Winterization Plan".

But it added that Israel would not permit the entry of equipment that could be used for military purposes by Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups.

An estimated 80% of all structures in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas, according to the UN.

More than 1.9 million people have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, it says.

The UN has warned that the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire despite the ceasefire agreed in October 2025, as Israeli air strikes and other attacks continue to hit populated areas, causing casualties and property damage and driving further displacement.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,640 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

articles.title: RILEY GAINES: Voters sent two midterm messages, and Democrats will only hear one
articles.summary: Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington backed women's sports protections even while electing Democrats in the midterm election.
articles.body: I’ll admit it. Tuesday night was disappointing. I expected Republicans to lose more seats than they flipped. History suggested as much. But I certainly didn’t expect the results to be quite that bad. Still, buried beneath the headlines celebrating Democratic victories was a rather inconvenient development for the political left. Americans may have voted to elect Democrats, but that doesn’t mean they’ve suddenly developed an appetite for the progressive social agenda again. FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS In fact, on one of the most contentious cultural issues of the last several years, voters delivered a remarkably consistent message. Keep men out of women’s sports. In Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington, voters backed measures protecting female athletic competition on the basis of biological sex. And these weren’t just Republican strongholds. Colorado and Washington are reliably blue states whose political leadership has spent years embracing progressive gender policies. Yet the same electorate willing to put Democrats in positions of power also voted to reject a central pillar of the modern progressive agenda. I don’t know how much clearer voters can make themselves. WASHINGTON STATE VOTERS APPEAR TO PASS FIRST-EVER BALLOT MEASURE SEPARATING BOYS AND GIRLS SPORTS For years, elected Democrats and their allies in the mainstream media have insisted that protecting women’s sports is an extreme position and that anyone who dares advocate for it is a hate-filled bigot. And believe me, that’s one of the nicer things I’ve been called. I understand why people are frustrated. Republicans should, too. We’ve been told that acknowledging biological differences between men and women is transphobic. That girls who object to sharing locker rooms or competing against male athletes are the problem. That sports should prioritize inclusion and kindness, even when doing so comes at the expense of fairness and safety. I’ve personally experienced what happens when you challenge that orthodoxy. I’ve also watched countless female athletes lose opportunities, endure public ridicule and face enormous pressure to remain silent simply for asking for something as basic as a fair shot. I’ve watched politicians, university administrators and athletic organizations bend themselves into knots trying to explain why women should be expected to sacrifice their own opportunities in the name of inclusion. WOMEN WHO FACED BIOLOGICAL MALES IN GIRLS' SPORTS AND LOCKER ROOMS SPEAK OUT AHEAD OF WASHINGTON STATE VOTE Voters made their position clear in 2024, when the Republican agenda prevailed nationally. Apparently, even after voting for Democrats in 2026, they still aren’t buying what the progressive left is selling on this issue. Consider Colorado. Opponents of the girls’ sports initiative reportedly raised roughly $4 million, with substantial backing from unions and progressive organizations, including Planned Parenthood. Proponents raised approximately $200,000, largely through grassroots efforts. They prevailed despite being outspent nearly 20 to 1. That’s a staggering disparity, and an even more telling result. At what point does the political left accept that this is a losing issue and give it a rest? Women’s sports protections are not some fringe position held exclusively by Republicans. The issue cuts across party lines, and the people who have spent years insisting otherwise have a serious problem on their hands. The cultural shift is evident well beyond the ballot box. Look at the response WNBA player Sophie Cunningham has received. LIZ PEEK: THERE MAY BE A SILVER LINING IN TRUMP'S BRUTAL MIDTERM DEFEAT After publicly expressing support for protecting women’s sports, Cunningham didn’t issue a groveling apology. She wasn’t shunned into professional exile. Quite the opposite. Her public profile exploded. Her social media following and engagement skyrocketed. Her merchandise became some of the most sought-after in the league, and her Adidas shoes reportedly sold out almost immediately. On Halloween, I saw countless young girls wearing her jersey and dressing up as Sophie Cunningham. The notion that expressing a common-sense view about women’s sports is automatically a career-ending offense looks increasingly ridiculous. For years, corporations, celebrities and athletes were conditioned to believe that stepping outside progressive orthodoxy would destroy their reputations. That threat doesn’t carry quite the same weight anymore. And I think that’s worth celebrating, particularly after an election that otherwise gave conservatives plenty of reasons to believe a serious reckoning is overdue. But there’s another part of Tuesday’s results that Republicans would be foolish to ignore. DEMOCRATS ARE CHANGING THEIR TRANSGENDER MESSAGE. REPUBLICANS SAY THEY’RE JUST FLIP-FLOPPING Affordability is a real problem. And I believe that was the bigger message voters sent on Tuesday by voting for Democrats. Americans are tired of working harder just to afford less. They’re tired of watching their grocery bills climb, calculating how much they can spend at the gas pump and wondering whether homeownership will ever be a realistic possibility. Young people, in particular, are confronting an economy that often feels stacked against them. And when they express their frustration, they’re too often dismissed as lazy or entitled. Sometimes that criticism is warranted. Most of the time, it isn’t. I believe Americans have remarkably short memories about just how bad inflation became under the Biden administration. But telling a struggling family that things used to be worse isn’t going to make their next grocery bill any easier to pay. People vote based on the lives they’re living, not just the economic statistics politicians would prefer they remember. And when people feel financially desperate, promises of sweeping government intervention can sound awfully attractive. That’s part of what makes socialism so dangerous. The promise of essentially free everything is appealing, particularly to generations that have never been adequately taught its historical consequences. Of course, nothing is actually free. The bill always comes due, whether through higher taxes, mounting debt or diminished economic opportunity. JACKSON THOMPSON: WASHINGTON STATE DEMOCRATIC PARTY CALLS GIRLS' SPORTS INITIATIVE UNCONSTITUTIONAL But dismissing every voter concerned about affordability as ignorant or entitled would be a serious mistake. I understand why people are frustrated. Republicans should, too. But I don’t think the voters’ message of "affordability" in voting for Democrats is what Democrats will hear. Elected Democrats will be tempted to interpret their victories as permission to expand DEI mandates, advance gender-transition policies for minors, allow boys access to the girls’ locker room, raise taxes, advocate for more lax immigration policies and continue placing ideological priorities ahead of the concerns of ordinary families. Those are two very different mandates. TREY GOWDY: THE MIDTERMS WERE A PAINFUL LESSON THAT REPUBLICANS CAN'T SKIP LEARNING Winning an election doesn’t mean voters have endorsed every plank of your platform. And it certainly doesn’t mean they’ve abandoned their common sense. Tuesday’s ballot initiatives should serve as a warning against making that assumption. They should also give Republican lawmakers in politically competitive states some much-needed confidence. Take Pennsylvania, where legislation protecting women’s sports has faced significant political resistance. For too long, some Republicans have treated this issue as politically radioactive, apparently convinced that defending female athletes is too controversial to be worth the fight. Well, voters in Colorado and Washington just offered a pretty compelling rebuttal. If these protections can earn majority support in states that routinely elect Democrats, what exactly are Republicans in purple states so afraid of? Of course, winning at the ballot box doesn’t mean the fight is over. MATT CALKINS: AFTER YEARS OF THREATS AND INTIMIDATION, THE BULLIES IN THE WOMEN'S SPORTS DEBATE FINALLY LOST Colorado’s newly elected Democratic governor, Phil Weiser, has already suggested that the state’s transgender-related ballot measures may need legislative adjustments. And we’ve seen elsewhere, including Maine, how officials such as Secretary of State Shanna Bellows have resisted efforts to restrict male participation in girls’ sports. I fully expect more legal challenges, political maneuvering and attempts to weaken these protections. But those efforts only reinforce the larger point. When the public is given a direct say, the progressive establishment doesn’t always like the answer. For a party that prides itself on defending democracy, it might consider respecting the democratic process even when the outcome is inconvenient. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION As for the next two years, Democrats will have an opportunity to show Americans what their governing priorities actually are. And if recent history is any indication, I suspect they’ll provide plenty of reminders of why voters rejected their national agenda in 2024. For some reason, this is the hill they continually choose to die on. Republicans, meanwhile, have work to do. They need to take affordability seriously, offer credible solutions and stop assuming that winning the cultural argument automatically translates into winning elections. It doesn’t. Voters can agree with you on cultural issues and still vote against you when they feel their financial concerns aren’t being addressed. Tuesday’s midterm election results proved that these realities can coexist, and Republicans would be wise to recognize it. Still, I refuse to confuse one disappointing election night with a wholesale cultural reversal. I’ve spent years speaking with parents, students and female athletes across the country. I’ve seen firsthand how much the conversation has changed. People who once whispered their concerns are increasingly willing to say them publicly. They’re less intimidated by the accusations, less willing to accept obvious contradictions and less interested in being lectured by institutions that have spent years squandering their trust. That’s not something that disappears because one party has a good election night. Political power changes hands. Cultural convictions are often much harder to reverse. Democrats won important elections Tuesday. Republicans should take those losses seriously, learn from them and make the necessary adjustments. But the voters also made something unmistakably clear once again. They haven’t suddenly decided that women and girls are undeserving of their own athletic categories, free from mediocre men. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP And if the progressive left believes Tuesday was a mandate to resurrect every unpopular cultural crusade Americans have spent years rejecting, they’re in for a rude awakening. Democrats may have won the election. They haven’t won the culture. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM RILEY GAINES

articles.title: Mariah Carey set to headline Powderham music festival in Devon
articles.summary: She is due to perform at Powderham Castle near Exeter in June 2027 with the Sugababes and Eternal.
articles.body:
Best-selling female solo artist Mariah Carey has been announced as the third headliner for a music festival.

Live at Powderham organisers said the singer would bring her Firefly summer tour to Powderham Castle in Devon on 27 June 2027, alongside special guests Sugababes, with additional support from R&B group Eternal.

The All I Want For Christmas Is You and Love Takes Time singer has amassed more than 19 Billboard Hot 100 Number One singles – more than any solo artist in history.

She is due to be headlining the festival near Exeter alongside Shania Twain, who has been set to perform on 24 June 2027; and Alex Warren, performing on 26 June .

Her recent performances included appearing at the opening ceremony of the 2026 Winter Olympics in Italy.

Live at Powderham attracted more than 140,000 people over its four days in 2026, with headline performances from Lewis Capaldi, Alanis Morissette and Teddy Swims.

The festival's final headliner has yet to be announced.

articles.title: Gaza authorities slam global ‘inaction’ after mudslide kills five people
articles.summary: Four children and a woman were killed after heavy rain caused a sandbank to collapse on their tent.
articles.body:
Palestinian authorities have criticised global “indifference and inaction” after a landslide killed five displaced people sheltering in tents in the central Gaza Strip following heavy rains.

“This is a scene that should shame the conscience of humanity and reflects the extent of the complicity and abandonment to which our […] people are subjected,” the Gaza Government Media Office said in a statement on Monday.

Four children and a woman were killed and two people remain missing after a sandbank collapsed onto their tent in Deir el-Balah on Sunday. The landslide happened after heavy rains brought by the first winter storm of the year hit the besieged territory on Friday, causing widespread flooding.

Floodwaters have inundated displacement camps and weakened buildings already damaged by Israeli air raids.

Restrictions imposed by the Israeli military mean specialist search and rescue equipment is in short supply, and Gaza residents were forced to dig using their bare hands to try and reach survivors.

Reporting from Deir el-Balah, Al Jazeera’s Tareq Abu Azzoum said the victims were living in flimsy tents, on exposed ground, with no protection from the heavy rain.

“When the embankment collapsed, those people had no chance to escape or protect themselves, and this raises difficult conditions about what people on the ground are left to endure,” he said.

About 70,000 tents were flooded when the storm hit Gaza at the weekend. According to data from Save the Children, more than half a million children are living in “critical or catastrophic” shelter conditions.

In a statement, Save the Children said, “While the so-called ceasefire announced over a year ago stipulated the entry of caravans as a more durable alternative to tents, Israeli authorities have repeatedly blocked their entry into Gaza, leaving hundreds of thousands of children exposed to another winter of hardship.”

The Government Media Office held Israel, the United States and the international community “fully and directly responsible”, citing their “absolute silence regarding the occupation’s crimes and their complicity in preventing the entry of shelter supplies, construction materials, caravans, fuel, and spare parts required to operate municipal and Civil Defence machinery and equipment”.

“We strongly condemn and denounce the state of inaction and the complete absence of the Board of Peace and the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, as though this catastrophe were of no concern to them. Their complete failure to act and their flagrant abdication of the responsibilities entrusted to them raise serious questions about the very purpose of these bodies, which remain passive observers in the face of the suffering of the Palestinian people.”

More than 74,600 people have been killed since Israel’s genocidal war began on October 7, 2023, in response to a Hamas-led attack on southern Israel. Since a “ceasefire” took effect in October 2025, Israel has killed more than 1,600 Palestinians.

articles.title: 39 dead as migrant boat capsizes off Senegal on perilous route to Spain's Canary Islands
articles.summary: At least 39 people have died after a boat carrying migrants capsized off the coast of Senegal while attempting to reach Spain's Canary Islands, according
articles.body: At least 39 people have died after a boat carrying migrants capsized off the coast of Senegal while attempting to reach Spain's Canary Islands, according to the Senegalese Press Agency (APS), which cited an official source.Senegal's interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was not yet known. Search operations were continuing after the small wooden vessel overturned between Dakar, the capital, and the northern city of Saint-Louis.Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told news agency AFP that all the bodies recovered so far were those of Senegalese nationals. The identities and nationalities of the remaining passengers were yet to be established.President Bassirou Diomaye Faye expressed condolences to the families of those who died and appealed to Senegalese citizens not to risk their lives on dangerous sea journeys.In a statement posted on X, he promised to step up action against the networks arranging these crossings."We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.Deadly Atlantic route to the Canary IslandsThe latest tragedy has once again drawn attention to the dangers faced by migrants attempting to reach Europe across the Atlantic.Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026. This was the highest death toll among the migration routes monitored by the organisation.Walking Borders estimated that around 21 people died for every 100 who successfully reached the Canary Islands during the period.The route has become increasingly prominent amid tighter border controls and greater cooperation between European countries and North African states. These measures may have pushed some migrants away from the central Mediterranean route and towards the Atlantic crossing.Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat on Friday, preventing 142 migrants from making the journey to Spain. The group included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the passengers were from Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.El Hierro declares emergency amid migrant arrivalsThe dangers of the Atlantic route have also coincided with a sharp rise in arrivals on Spain's Canary Islands.Authorities on the Spanish island of El Hierro declared a state of emergency on Saturday after more than 3,300 migrants arrived in around 30 boats since the beginning of November.The number of arrivals is equivalent to almost a third of the island's population. El Hierro is one of the main entry points into Europe for migrants travelling by sea from West Africa.Fernando Clavijo, president of the Canary Islands regional government, described the situation as "absolutely unsustainable," according to Reuters.Unemployment drives migrationLimited job opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the reasons prompting people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).For many young people, the possibility of finding employment and earning more in Europe remains a strong incentive, despite the risk of undertaking the dangerous journey in overcrowded boats.Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.The figures underline the employment challenge facing President Faye's government. He came to power in 2024 with overwhelming support from a predominantly young electorate and has faced pressure to create opportunities for them.In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's Interior Ministry said it would continue its efforts to dismantle people-smuggling networks, including through stronger cooperation with neighbouring countries.You use AI every day. articles.title: Russia-Ukraine peace talks: From territorial disputes to Nato - key issues on Abu Dhabi agenda
articles.summary: Russia, Ukraine and the United States are set to discuss security guarantees, territorial disputes and a wider European security framework when their
articles.body: Russia, Ukraine and the United States are set to discuss security guarantees, territorial disputes and a wider European security framework when their negotiators meet in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. The two-day round of peace talks are aimed at ending the nearly five-year-old war. The negotiations, the first trilateral meeting since February, come amid continued fighting along the front line and escalating Russian and Ukrainian drone and missile attacks.The talks follow months of stalled diplomatic efforts. Previous rounds of negotiations earlier this year failed to make visible progress towards ending Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II. With Moscow and Kyiv holding sharply different positions on the terms of a settlement, the discussions are expected to focus on the security arrangements that could prevent another escalation, as well as the territorial and military issues standing in the way of a peace deal.Here is what will be on the agenda:Security guarantees for Ukraine and RussiaSecurity guarantees are expected to be a central focus of the Abu Dhabi negotiations. Ukraine wants assurances from Western allies that would deter Russia from launching another invasion after a potential peace agreement.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Kyiv and its allies have discussed guarantees similar to NATO's Article 5. Under the provision, an attack on one NATO member is treated as an attack against the entire alliance.In an interview broadcast on November 5, Zelenskyy said the key question was how Western countries would respond if Russia attacked Ukraine again.“If Russia starts again, what will happen?” Zelenskyy asked. “Who will do what, with what means, and when?”Some European countries have also considered deploying troops to Ukraine after a potential peace deal. However, Moscow has rejected the proposal and warned that any European troops on Ukrainian soil would be treated as legitimate targets.Russia, meanwhile, wants security guarantees of its own. The Kremlin has long opposed NATO's military presence in Central and Eastern Europe, arguing that the alliance's deployments threaten Russian security.Before launching its full-scale invasion in 2022, Moscow had demanded that NATO roll back its troop and weapons deployments in the region. Similar demands are likely to feature in any comprehensive settlement proposed by Russia.US President Donald Trump has also hinted at a wider agreement on European security. After meeting Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House on November 4, Trump said a broader deal was being discussed.“It's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine,” Trump said, adding that it might include all of Europe.Territorial disputes and military restrictionsThe territorial question remains one of the biggest obstacles to a peace agreement.Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to withdraw its troops from four regions that Moscow illegally annexed during the war but has never fully captured. He also wants Kyiv to abandon its ambition of joining NATO, accept strict limits on its military and lift restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.Putin has insisted on a comprehensive peace agreement based on these conditions. He has rejected a general ceasefire, arguing that it would give Ukrainian forces time to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles.Zelenskyy, however, has refused to surrender Ukrainian territory that Russian forces have failed to capture on the battlefield. Kyiv is also opposed to restrictions on its military and its security arrangements with Western partners.Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire should be the first step towards a broader settlement. It has also maintained that territorial disputes can only be resolved through a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy.Role of European countries in negotiationsThe participation of European countries is another point of disagreement between Moscow and Kyiv.Ukraine wants its European allies to be part of the negotiations, arguing that any agreement on the continent's security must involve the countries directly affected by it.Russia, however, has opposed their participation in the Abu Dhabi meeting.“No one is going to invite them to the negotiating table,” Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said when asked whether European envoys could join the talks. He added that even if they travelled to Abu Dhabi, they would not be allowed into the negotiating room.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said European countries would have to be involved in broader discussions at a later stage.“Since the discussion will touch upon the future security architecture in Europe while addressing the mutual security of Russia and Ukraine, at some stage it would be impossible to do it without the Europeans,” he said.European involvement has also been complicated by the European Union's difficulty in deciding who should represent the bloc in negotiations with Moscow.On October 27, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke to Putin in their first known direct conversations with the Russian leader since shortly after the 2022 invasion. They said they had spoken as leaders of Russia's Nordic neighbours and not on behalf of the European Union.Peskov criticised the bloc's inability to appoint a representative, saying EU members “can't even decide yet who is authorised to speak on their behalf”. He described it as “a protracted indecisiveness and a lack of readiness on its part.”Long-term European security frameworkBeyond ending the fighting in Ukraine, the US has indicated that the negotiations could address wider security arrangements between Russia and Europe.Zelenskyy said on November 4 that he had held a 90-minute conversation with US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law. He said the negotiations “must move forward at full throttle to bring this war to an end as quickly as possible.”Kushner said the objective was to address the security concerns of all sides and reduce the possibility of future conflicts.“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” he said in a post on X.He also highlighted the need for a broader framework to address decades of tensions between Russia and European countries.“For over 30 years, “Europe and Russia have struggled to establish a sustainable security framework,” Kushner wrote. “Decades of mistrust, competing security concerns, and the devastating consequences of this war make this an extraordinarily difficult challenge, but one that is essential to lasting peace.”He identified the main objectives as “permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.”Russia's hardline position and continued fightingThe negotiations will take place against the backdrop of continued fighting and growing attacks on critical infrastructure.Russia has intensified strikes on Ukraine's power grid as winter approaches. Moscow has increasingly used ballistic missiles and faster, jet-powered drones, while Ukraine faces shortages of US-made Patriot air defence interceptors.Zelenskyy said last week that “every power plant in Ukraine has been damaged in one way or another by attacks”. He urged Kyiv's allies to provide generators and other equipment to maintain electricity supplies. He also called on them to share their air defence stockpiles, with Ukraine offering to help replenish them later.Putin has repeatedly warned that Russia will pursue its objectives through military force if Kyiv refuses to accept Moscow's terms.Russia's chief negotiator, presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky, is also expected to represent Moscow in the talks. Medinsky, a former culture minister, led Russia's delegation during the first direct peace negotiations with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022.Known for his hardline views, he made a pointed remark during the 2025 Istanbul talks, reportedly saying that Peter the Great had taken 21 years to defeat Sweden in the 18th century and that Moscow was prepared to fight for as long as necessary.The latest diplomatic push follows a weeklong localised truce around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine last month. Brokered with the help of US first lady Melania Trump, it allowed some residents to evacuate and humanitarian supplies to reach the area.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: At least 21 migrants and refugees die trying to reach Greece’s Crete
articles.summary: Greece’s coastguard said more than 100 people rescued in several operations off the southern coast of Crete.
articles.body:
At least 21 people have died while trying to reach the Greek island of Crete, a key hub for refugees and migrants trying to reach Europe, authorities said.

The Greek coastguard said it recovered 12 bodies and rescued 18 people from one boat that was spotted by a Morocco-flagged container ship south of the island early on Monday. It said it had taken the survivors and the dead to shore. One person taken to hospital later died.

It was not immediately clear what had caused the deaths but Greek authorities said the boat may have been at sea for days, struggling to reach the shore due to strong winds.

In a separate incident, the Greek coastguard recovered eight bodies and rescued 28 refugees and migrants from a boat off southern Crete on Saturday evening. Two people are still missing.

Two other boats, one carrying about 47 people and another with about 40 people on board, were also found sailing south of Crete.

The European Union’s border agency Frontex used an aircraft and an unmanned drone to locate the boats, before taking survivors to a port on the southern coast of Crete.

Crete has become one of the main entry points into the EU for people fleeing conflict and poverty in the Middle East, Africa and Asia.

Frontex said irregular border crossings into the bloc were down by a third so far this year.

The agency said that about 31,800 crossings were recorded in the first three quarters of 2026, a fall of 15 percent compared with the same period last year.

articles.title: Congress returns with big to-do list and how Ukraine is using AI on the battlefield: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: Congress returns with a big to-do list. How Ukraine is using AI against Russia. And tension in Philadelphia over a boycott targeting Jewish-owned restaurants.
articles.body: Congress returns with a big to-do list after a Democratic sweep of the midterms. Nvidia opens an investigation after its CEO’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. And condemnation in Philadelphia over a boycott targeting Jewish-owned restaurants. Here’s what to know today. Big tasks await as Congress returns after Democratic wins Congress returns today after a blue tsunami in the midterms swept Democrats into control of both chambers. But first, they have a lame-duck session to get through with Republicans still in charge — and a tall list of tasks to complete. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Here are some of the top items: → Fund the government: Lawmakers have to avert a shutdown on Dec. 11. Many were hoping to approve a full-year appropriations bill, but that’s far from certain as Iran war funding emerges as a flash point. → House leadership races: House Republicans will choose their leadership team tomorrow in a secret-ballot election. Speaker Mike Johnson’s departure sets up a race for minority leader between Reps. Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan. → Hegseth impeachment: Rep. Thomas Massie said he will reintroduce articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of the eight-month war with Iran. Read the full list here. More politics news: Trump said that his immigration policies were “too tough,” saying in an interview on CBS’ “60 Minutes” that mass deportations hurt him during the midterm elections. The president said he was “only kidding” when he offered the job of White House press secretary to UFC head Dana White. The future of AI warfare is playing out on Ukraine’s battlefields Ukraine has embraced AI in the war to gain an advantage against Russia, turning its military into battlefield beta testers. In interviews with NBC News, officials and entrepreneurs offered a rare glimpse at how the technology is being integrated. One AI tool interacts with a digital twin of the battlefield, turning front-line data into recommendations for commanders to formulate scenarios. Another model analyzes images from reconnaissance drones, finding key details that can help hunt down the enemy. In a David-versus-Goliath fight, Ukrainians believe developments like these can even out the asymmetry. “We are convinced that the future of war — no matter how scary it sounds — is a war of operating systems,” said the leader of a Defense Ministry center. More exclusive reporting. Tensions rise in Philadelphia over boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants A bike ride organized to promote a boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants drew opposing demonstrators to Philadelphia yesterday, with people waving Palestinian and Israeli flags exchanging heated words. articles.title: Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assaults
articles.summary: British comedian and actor Russell Brand was in court for sentencing on Monday, days after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault.
articles.body: LONDON — British comedian and actor Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for rape and sexual assault by a London court on Monday. The lengthy prison term completes a stunning fall from grace for Brand, 51, who found fame on both sides of the Atlantic chronicling his promiscuity and battles with addiction. He was found guilty Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He had pleaded not guilty to all counts and denied all of the allegations. Brand appeared in the London court Monday wearing a dark suit and at times making a sign of the cross, as the judge, Justice Joel Bennathan, called him a “sexual predator” before delivering his sentence. The judge had warned last week that Brand faced a “significant” prison term for his crimes. Stressing that he had to be careful not to punish Brand more “because you are famous,” the judge also paid tribute to the “determination and bravery” of the women who testified against him. “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent,” he added. Under English law, the maximum sentence for rape is life imprisonment, and 10 years for one count of sexual assault, according to Britain’s sentencing council. Brand’s female victims told the court Monday — in person and in written statements — that they were still living with the trauma and effects in their daily lives. “I’ve been in shock and turmoil for years,” one woman told the sentencing hearing, while another said he appeared to show “no remorse.” Victims of alleged sexual offenses are granted anonymity for life under British law. Since Brand’s conviction, London’s Metropolitan Police said it had provided prosecutors with investigations into two more rape allegations against him. Asked by reporters whether he had a message for the victims as he left court, Brand’s father Ron Brand said he didn’t care about them and suggested they had “chased and harassed” his son. He added that he didn’t believe in the justice system “on the basis of what I just watched.” Brand’s case has renewed scrutiny on the ethics of the entertainment industry, through which Brand rose from a flamboyant British broadcaster and stand-up comedian to a star of Hollywood movies. After the four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London, a jury of eight men and four women found Brand guilty of having raped a female fan at his home after she met him at one of his shows in 2009. He was also found guilty of sexually assaulting a woman whose breasts he grabbed at a party in 2004, and another woman who said he had kissed and groped her at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005. A third guilty verdict was delivered to Brand for the sexual assault of a woman who testified that he had pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an advertisement in 2009. He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault. Prosecutors said the women do not know one another and that they separately went to police after a TV documentary was broadcast in Britain in 2023. During the trial, prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones called Brand a ruthless, calculating, manipulative “sexual predator” who treated women as a “disposable commodity.” Brand admitted in his testimony to being sex-obsessed as a young and famous man. He denied ever having nonconsensual sex. At the height of his fame, Brand featured in several Hollywood movies, including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek.” His fame stateside was cemented when he briefly wed singer Katy Perry in a lavish ceremony in India in 2010. The couple divorced in 2012. Brand’s current wife, Laura Gallacher, was in the courtroom Monday and had previously testified that he was a “caring, kind and a wonderful father.” The couple married in 2017 and have three young children. In recent years, Brand had moved away from mainstream media, becoming an anti-establishment commentator. He briefly relocated to Florida and has built a large online following with videos that discuss U.S. politics, wellness, conspiracy theories and his newfound Christian faith. Speaking after the sentencing, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy told reporters that the sentence marked “a significant milestone in our investigation and means Russell Brand has been held accountable for his crimes.” Praising the victims, he said: “Reporting sexual offences can be incredibly difficult, and they have shown immense bravery, dignity and resilience throughout what has been a lengthy investigation and challenging trial process. “The victims have had to revisit deeply traumatic experiences and endure significant public and media attention. I hope today’s outcome provides some measure of closure and allows them to continue rebuilding their lives.” If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.

articles.title: Russia-Ukraine war: Nine Zimbabweans caught trying to leave South Africa to join conflict
articles.summary: Hundreds of people from different African countries have been recruited to fight for Russia, according to Ukraine.
articles.body:
Nine Zimbabweans have been arrested in South Africa after they were caught allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia and the Ukraine, police say.

The group, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in and around Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team on Sunday evening.

They were caught as they were "preparing to board flights out of the country", authorities added, but their final destination is unclear.

They have been charged with contravening South Africa's Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which outlaws mercenary activity without government permission.

Police said five people were arrested at South Africa's biggest airport, OR Tambo, and another four at a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team that involved Interpol.

All nine later appeared in court, according to state prosecutors.

The police statement added that the involvement of Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies indicated that the suspects had also allegedly violated laws in their respective home countries, prompting cooperation with South African authorities.

They have also not said whether the group allegedly intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine nor provided details of the organisations allegedly involved in facilitating their travel.

Citizens of several African countries, including Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, have gone to fight for Russia in Ukraine - some they had been duped and had not realised where they were going.

A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.

Kenya at the time estimated that 252 citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia. In March, Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue.

He said at the time that an agreement had been reached to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.

In March, Zimbabwe said that 15 of its nationals had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia in Ukraine, with more than 60 still trapped on the frontlines.

The previous month, South Africa secured the return of 17 South Africans who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.

In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.

Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.

articles.title: Trump says ‘great dislike’ for Israel contributed to Republican midterm losses
articles.summary: The president’s comments underscore a sea change in US politics where Israel once had bipartisan support.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said a “great dislike” for Israel was one of the reasons the Republicans lost in the midterm elections, along with the Iran war and the subsequent rise in gasoline prices. “I think if I was on the ballot, it would’ve been a much different situation because you saw the level of popularity and love,” Trump said in an interview with CBS’ “60 Minutes” that aired Sunday. “But there’s something beyond that. They didn’t like the war. They didn’t like the fact that gasoline went up, ‘cause I had it down at a low, and there’s a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel.” Trump’s comments underscore a sea change in US politics where Israel once had bipartisan support, as well as strong backing from Republican and Democratic presidents. But the extent of US military and financial support for Israel emerged as a frequent political liability during the midterm elections. Michigan’s Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed may have been the most prominent critic of Israel during the elections, but he was far from the only one. Even Vice President JD Vance suggested Republicans would have to rethink their once-stalwart support of Israel moving forward. Trump said he agrees with Vance’s position that the war with Iran is among the reasons for the Republican loss. But he said he doesn’t regret his decision to launch the war. “You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon. I think, historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not. But you know, I have to go with what’s right for our country. If they had a nuclear weapon during my term, I would be excoriated far worse than what’s happened.” The president also said that other countries, including Israel, would have to share the costs of the war. “Those countries that we’ve protected are going to pay us back any and all costs that we’ve had for the war ‘cause without us, they wouldn’t exist. Without us, Israel would not exist,” Trump said. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has long presented himself as the leader best able to manage the relationship with the United States and particularly Trump. But in just a matter of days, Trump has signaled major changes may be coming. “Democrats and Republicans are competing to see who can distance themselves from us more,” wrote Israeli journalist Amir Tibon on X. “And if we don’t act quickly, the new Congress will start holding up arms sales.” Tibon called for a new government that can begin “repairing the damage Netanyahu is leaving behind.” On the day of the US elections, Trump said he would end $4 billion in annual aid to Israel this year, potentially cutting off one of the key elements of Israel’s security strategy. Days later, Netanyahu said the aid would shift to a “partnership,” but didn’t say whether Trump had given him a heads-up about the surprise announcement. Israeli President Isaac Herzog made an oblique reference to the shift in American and international perceptions of the country on Sunday, as he tasked Netanyahu’s rival, Gadi Eizenkot, with forming the next government. “The challenges facing the State of Israel are immense. Some demand urgent and immediate attention,” he said. “Iran does not pause for a moment in its schemes and threats. We must work to build a diplomatic horizon in the region and for the day after the war.”

articles.title: Mysterious blood-soaked relic linked to history's most beloved saint, St Francis of Assisi, goes on display
articles.summary: An 800-year-old blood relic from St. Francis of Assissi is now on display in San Francisco, California, marking the first time the sacred artifact has left Italy.
articles.body: Christians visiting San Francisco have a rare opportunity to see an 800-year-old relic believed to contain the blood of one of history's most beloved saints, St. Francis of Assisi — marking the first time the artifact has left Italy. The relics of the saint are currently on display at the Cathedral of St. Mary of the Assumption until Nov. 28. The display commemorates the 800th anniversary of the death of Francis, who lived from approximately 1181 to 1226. LOST CITY IN AREA TIED TO BIBLICAL EXODUS MAY HAVE FINALLY BEEN DISCOVERED IN EGYPT The saint is best known for founding the Franciscan Order, as well as for being the patron saint of animals. The exhibition includes a painted panel of the saint dating to around 1290 — but the crown jewel of the display is the Bandage Relic of the Stigmata of Saint Francis of Assisi, a centuries-old cloth believed to contain his blood. Pictures of the relic on display show that the blood on the bandage still appears intensely red, even 800 years later. The relics' arrival in San Francisco carries particular significance because the city was named after St. Francis, said Candida Moss, the Edward Cadbury professor of theology at the University of Birmingham. SACRED PAGES OF 1,000-YEAR-OLD GOSPEL REVEAL ANCIENT DNA SCIENTISTS NEVER EXPECTED "People love St. Francis, but Francis isn't just venerated by Catholics," Moss told Fox News Digital, noting that he is also revered by Orthodox Christians, Anglicans and Lutherans. "I think this will become temporarily a pilgrimage site," she added. Moss said St. Francis' enduring popularity stems from his extraordinary transformation from a wealthy young man to someone who devoted his life to serving the poor. "He starts off just like everyone else. He wanted to be a knight," she said. "And then he changes his life. He ministers to the poor. He has all of these stories about him preaching to birds." ANCIENT CHRISTIAN AMULET UNEARTHED AFTER 1,500 YEARS MAY HOLD BIBLICAL SECRET "These are all really endearing stories about a man devoted to God," added Moss. The bloodstained bandages are tied to another defining moment in St. Francis' life, when he reportedly experienced a vision of a seraph, a six-winged angel, and received the stigmata — wounds resembling those suffered by Jesus Christ during the crucifixion. "He then has these wounds for the rest of his life that link him on a spiritual level to Christ," Moss said. "And so there are so many elements of this story, the miraculous, the sentimental, the relatable, that I think make Francis one of the most popular medieval saints, if not the most popular medieval saint." LOST PAGES WITH 'GHOST' TEXT RECOVERED FROM ONE OF THE WORLD'S MOST IMPORTANT NEW TESTAMENT MANUSCRIPTS The exhibition also raises questions about how centuries-old religious relics are preserved and authenticated, Moss said. While St. Francis' relics have a documented chain of custody dating back to the monastery where he died, Moss said some objects previously attributed to the saint have turned out to be inauthentic. "This is a really important part of church history, and it's worth seeing for yourself." One example is a tunic once believed to have belonged to St. Francis that was housed in Florence. Carbon dating revealed that the garment was from about 150 years after his lifetime. Moss suggested the garment was likely a "pious forgery" that had been mistakenly identified as a relic. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Although some of St. Francis' other relics have been carbon-dated to the appropriate historical period, the bloodstained bandage currently on display has not undergone such testing, according to Moss. The reason the blood on the centuries-old bandage still appears red remains unclear. "Now, for religious people, the explanation might be [that] this is miraculous in some way," Moss said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "But there has been no scrutiny of this particular relic, which is the most important of the Francis relics," she added. "So we can't really say for certain why it is that it seems so well-preserved." Despite the unanswered questions about the relic's preservation, Moss emphasized the rarity of the exhibition and its importance to church history. "You can't acquire anything like this," she said. "You couldn't buy it on eBay, because it is against church protocols to buy this. And this is the first time that these relics have left Italy." articles.title: Judo star Teddy Riner announces a run for French president, pledging to bring people together
articles.summary: Judo star Teddy Riner wants to be the next French president.
articles.body: Judo star Teddy Riner wants to be the next French president. The 37-year-old multiple Olympic champion, who is consistently ranked among France’s favorite public figures, announced his bid on social media on Monday. Riner, who has liberal economic views, said in an interview with Le Parisien newspaper that he is positioning himself as “neither right-wing nor left-wing” and hopes to become a “president who brings people together.” Asked whether his bid should be taken seriously, Riner said “what would be irresponsible would be to remain silent and stand by as a spectator to what is happening in our country, and what has been happening for several years now.” The French presidential election is being held next year, and campaigning is taking place in a tense social climate. Protest marches have been drawing huge crowds for weeks in Paris and elsewhere across France as demonstrators demand higher wages and back the country’s student protest movement, piling fresh pressure on the beleaguered government. Riner said he is aware of the social tensions running through the country and that he can’t accept young people and older generations saying they are struggling to imagine a future for themselves. “I hear the anger, which some people echo in their rhetoric with a great deal of negativity, coming from people who no longer have any ambition or the desire to think big,” Riner said. “Yet France is a great country. It has allowed me to become the person I am today and given me the opportunity to dream big. Today, that is precisely what is missing. There is no longer that ambition, no longer that hope.” Riner said in September that he wants to end his stellar career with a fourth individual Olympic gold medal at the Los Angeles Games in 2028. Asked by Le Parisien if his presidential bid means he is giving up on the Olympics, the 6-foot-8 heavyweight said no. “Not if my duties as president allow it and the French people give me their blessing,” the 11-time world champion said. French authorities in September said they investigated online racial abuse aimed at Riner after he expressed concern about the rise of the far right. In an interview with French sports television show Stade 2, Riner said he was “freaked out” by the rise of extremism. Asked if he meant “on both sides” — meaning the far left and far right — Riner replied “the far right.” According to opinion polls, the nationalist Marine Le Pen is the front-runner to replace Emmanuel Macron, ahead of hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Other aspirants include two former prime ministers of Macron. Candidates from the moderate left and right, the Green party and conservatives, are also running, among others. “The country is experiencing deep divisions right now, let’s not kid ourselves,” Riner said. “And in the face of that, I don’t see a single candidate putting forward a credible and fair vision capable of bringing the French people together rather than dividing them. There is no one today offering genuine, sincere hope. It’s always one side against another. I’m running for president to show that we can get France back on its feet. We are capable of achieving great things together.” In order to stand, Riner will need to gather 500 sponsorship signatures from elected officials, as required by French law. Asked about what would be his first initiative on the international stage if he is elected, Riner said he wants to make sure France works well with its allies and commands greater respect. “A lot of people around me have been talking about my first handshake with Donald Trump,” he said, laughing. “We’ll see who has the firmer handshake.”
