articles.title: Thirteen migrants die after boat sinks off Crete
articles.summary: The Greek coastguard says it has rescued 18 people, all of whom were Sudanese nationals.
articles.body:
At least 13 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of the Greek island of Crete.

The coastguard said it had rescued 18 people, all of whom were Sudanese nationals. Four of the survivors were taken to hospital, including a toddler.

Authorities said it was not immediately clear what caused the deaths, but they believe the boat had been at sea for days and had struggled to reach shore due to strong winds.

Crete remains one of several key gateways for migrants attempting to reach Europe from the Middle East and North Africa, with more than 22,000 of the 86,400 sea arrivals so far this year landing in Crete alone.

One unnamed coastguard official who spoke to news agency Reuters on condition of anonymity said the survivors were "shivering from the cold".

The migrants' boat was spotted by a Moroccan-flagged container ship about 15 nautical miles (28km) off Crete's coast.

The Greek coastguard rescued another 187 people in three separate incidents off the coast of Greece on Monday.

More than 37,000 migrants have arrived in Greece so far this year, UN figures show, already surpassing the number who arrived in the entirety of 2025.

The Greek government has announced plans to deal with the influx, including opening a temporary housing complex near the Cretan capital, Heraklion.

Greece was at the heart of Europe's migration crisis in 2015-16, when nearly a million people arrived on its islands, mostly from Turkey.

Arrivals later fell as border controls tightened, but crossings from Libya have surged in recent years, particularly among people fleeing conflict in Sudan and seeking better economic opportunities from countries including Bangladesh.

articles.title: Beth Holloway recalls the moment she came face to face with daughter Natalee’s killer in 2005: ‘He knows’
articles.summary: Every morning before she leaves for work, Beth Holloway makes sure to kiss the senior portrait of her late daughter, Natalee Holloway, to give her thanks for the strength she still provides her on a daily basis.
articles.body: Every morning before she leaves for work, Beth Holloway makes sure to kiss the senior portrait of her late daughter, Natalee Holloway, to give her thanks for the strength she still provides her on a daily basis. Beth Holloway spoke with NBC News correspondent Sam Brock for a segment that aired on TODAY Nov. 9 about what her life is like now that she finally received the answers she desperately sought for nearly two decades about her daughter’s disappearance and death in Aruba. “The weight of the world has been lifted off me,” she said. “I spent 18 years in the dark. I just couldn’t see it. I couldn’t find it. I couldn’t hear it, and so I’d waited 18 years, and it’s horrible that that’s the news I get. Families need to know the answers, no matter how brutal they are.” The grandmother of two has resumed her work as a speech pathologist at an Alabama public school after taking nine years off to pursue the truth about her daughter’s death. “I was determined by hope, and I was driven by love, and the love for my daughter, and to find out the answers to what happened to her, and I was acting on faith,” Beth Holloway said. “And when you do those three things, you can accomplish a lot.” Her relentless quest to find out what happened to her 18-year-old daughter during an Aruba vacation in 2005 is detailed in the new three-part Netflix docuseries, “Taken: Natalee Holloway.” In 2023, Dutch citizen Joran van der Sloot confessed to killing the Alabama teen on a beach in Aruba in 2005 and pushing her body out to sea when he was 17 years old.’ “I finally have a conclusion,” Beth Holloway said about doing the documentary, in which she was featured. “There’s a finale. It took me 18 years to get the answers, but justice takes a lot of work, and I felt like now’s the time to tell, for the first time, a comprehensive and conclusive story of what happened to Natalee and her journey of 20 years.” Natalee Holloway met van der Sloot for the first time within hours after she arrived in Aruba in 2005 when Natalee went missing. She described their first meeting to Brock. “My initial interaction with Joran was another moment of, ‘He knows. He knows what happened to her,’” Beth Holloway said. She is hoping viewers of the docuseries can take away two things from it. “I’d like for them to see the capacity of faith to carry you through the most difficult times,” she said. “You have to be determined by hope.” The other message she wants to deliver is people minding their safety while traveling. Natalee was seen by friends and on surveillance footage leaving a bar in Aruba late at night in a car with van der Sloot and two brothers and then was never seen again. “I want to make sure that they’re also seeing why they do need to be mindful and make a plan, because that’s why I spent the last 18 to 20 years pounding the podiums, because we can never have too many safety reminders,” Beth Holloway said. When he confessed in 2023 to killing Natalee Holloway, van der Sloot was already in the midst of a 28-year prison sentence in Peru after being convicted of murdering 21-year-old Peruvian woman Stephany Flores in 2010. He made the confession in 2023 as part of a proffer agreement in a separate wire fraud and extortion case in Alabama after he was extradited from Peru. “That day was a long time coming,” Beth Holloway said. “The torturous part is the not knowing, and as shocking and as torturous as it is to hear this, it is finally a relief to know that’s what I had been searching for for 18 years. I had to know, no matter how brutal it was. I needed to know what happened.” Beth Holloway’s attorney, John Q. Kelly, says in the Netflix documentary that van der Sloot contacted him in 2010 in a bid to extort $250,000 from the Holloway family in exchange for information about where they could find Natalee Holloway’s body. Previously unseen FBI surveillance footage of van der Sloot meeting in Aruba with Kelly to arrange a $25,000 down payment is shown in the docuseries. Once van der Sloot’s information about where Natalee Holloway’s body was located turned out to be bogus, prosecutors said, Beth Holloway sued him for wire fraud and extortion in an Alabama court. As part of the proffer agreement, his 20-year sentence for the Alabama charges was allowed to be served concurrently with his prison sentence in Peru, where he is currently incarcerated. Van der Sloot, who is now 39, is eligible for parole in Peru in 2045, but Beth Holloway told Brock she is not done pursuing justice against him for her daughter. She said she is working with Netherlands attorneys Royce de Vries and Annemiek van Spanje to file a murder complaint against van der Sloot with Dutch prosecutors in the Netherlands. Her hope is he could be extradited to the Netherlands at the end of his sentence in Peru, face trial on charges of Natalee Holloway’s murder and potentially serve a sentence in a Dutch prison. Nearly three years after hearing van der Sloot confess to killing her daughter, Beth Holloway says she feels “so much of Natalee” in her family. “I’m constantly calling my grandchildren Natalee and Matt, constantly the wrong names, and that’s probably more common than not,” she says, adding that she feels her daughter’s life “realigning” with her children. “It’s a great sense of peace,” she said. She also says she’s able to spend time with her daughter’s friends, which is a “blessing.” “The one silver lining though in that fight is, and what I wish everyone could realize is, you’re on a healing path, and you don’t even know it,” she added. “And as hard as it is, it would be more painful not to get on that path than to look back 20 years and have regrets. I live my life with no regrets, no step wasted.” She makes sure to give her daughter’s photo a kiss before work to let her know she’s not forgotten. “She’s thought of every single day,” Beth Holloway said.

articles.title: ‘No concession’: What to expect from Russia-US-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.summary: A fourth round of peace talks in 2026 takes place this week, with security guarantees high on the agenda.
articles.body:
Officials from Ukraine, Russia and the United States are set to converge in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), for negotiations aimed at ending nearly five years of war between Moscow and Kyiv.

But analysts are not hopeful of much progress in the trilateral talks slated for Tuesday and Wednesday amid US President Donald Trump’s recent engagement with the Kremlin.

Trump has blamed President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for holding up peace efforts. “Zelenskyy has to want to settle this war, and if he doesn’t, I think it’s going to be a very bad thing,” he said last month. The US also signed a deal last month to buy Russian diesel, which critics say would provide Russia with revenue to sustain the war against Ukraine.

On Thursday, Trump claimed that the war was close to being settled , and ending it might involve all of Europe. But Europe is not officially part of the trilateral talks. Last week, France said that Europe will send representatives to Abu Dhabi, as Ukraine’s Western allies fear Trump might force a deal that might undermine the continent’s security.

Russia occupies roughly 20 percent of Ukraine, including Crimea and parts of the eastern Donbas region. The Russian move has not been recognised by the international community, but Trump has urged Kyiv to cede territory for a deal to end the war that has killed thousands and displaced millions.

So what can we expect from the latest round of peace talks this year, as tit-for-tat attacks on energy sites have intensified in recent months? The two sides have held three rounds of US-mediated peace talks this year, including two in Abu Dhabi.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will be heading the US delegation for the first such talks in nine months, as the US president has pushed to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.

Ukraine’s primary negotiator and foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov will lead Kyiv’s negotiation team, the Kyiv Independent reported. The Ukrainian delegation will also include David Arakhamia, head of Zelenskyy’s parliamentary group; Zelenskyy’s chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov; and Sergiy Kyslytsya, first deputy head of the Presidential Office.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, meanwhile, confirmed last week that the Russian delegation would be led by former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky, the state news agency TASS reported. It also includes diplomat Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yuri Zhygarlovsky, the Kremlin said.

On Monday, the Kremlin said the peace talks would not include European officials. Peskov’s comments to reporters appeared to conflict with a statement on Sunday by French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, who said officials from France, Britain, Germany, NATO and the European Commission would be present at the November 10-11 meeting.

An EU official told the AFP news agency on Monday that national security officials for the bloc, NATO, France, Germany and the United Kingdom would be on site – but it was unclear how they would be involved.

What is at stake in the Abu Dhabi talks?

“I don’t expect any tangible progress in the Abu Dhabi talks. The reason is simple and remains the same – Putin has absolutely no intention to negotiate seriously. He remains totally fixated on the [destruction] of Ukraine,” Oleksandr Merezhko, a Ukrainian member of parliament from the Servant of the People party, told Al Jazeera.

Putin wants Ukraine’s “surrender”, which will allow him to subjugate Ukrainians, he said.

Finnish-Russian political scientist Arkady Moshes says Ukraine’s sovereignty and independence are at stake in the upcoming talks.

Restoring Ukrainian territorial integrity, including Crimea, may already be beyond reach, said Moshes, a programme director at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs. Russia annexed the Crimean peninsula in 2014 – a move not recognised by the United Nations.

Moshes said that it would be very difficult for Ukraine to accept a peace agreement that doesn’t allow it “to choose its alliances, decide on its security future, or [that] put limits on its military”.

Ukraine wants Russia to withdraw from its territory and a security guarantee as part of any deal with Russia, but Russia has refused to end its occupation and set conditions that Kyiv should not be given membership of the NATO alliance. Moscow has also opposed the deployment of foreign troops in Ukraine after a deal.

Matthew Boyse, a senior fellow with Hudson Institute’s Center on Europe and Eurasia specialising in Central Europe, agreed that the most difficult sticking points are those about territory and security guarantees for Ukraine.

“So far Putin has not budged from his ‘my way or the highway’ and ‘what’s mine is mine and what’s yours is negotiable’ position,” Boyse, a former US diplomat, told Al Jazeera.

The analysts agreed that the future of European security as a whole is also at stake.

“The Kremlin agreed to and codified the post-1991 European security order in many agreements and treaties until Putin in the 2000s began to tear them up and in 2014 turned that order upside down,” said Boyse, referring to Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014.

But the Kremlin has accused the US and its European allies of encircling Russia militarily. To that end, Russia has opposed the expansion of NATO in Europe, which it sees as a security threat. Russia has warned of a direct military standoff with Europe if NATO expands its military footprint eastward closer to the Russian border.

Anders Olofsgard, deputy director at the Stockholm Institute of Transition Economics, said it was reassuring that Kushner had explicitly stated that “NATO would remain central to European collective defence and that no country should have a veto over another country’s security or alliance choices”.

Another element at stake is the future of post-Soviet states in Europe, namely Belarus, Moldova, Georgia and Armenia, said Moshes, the political scientist.

“If Ukraine now capitulates despite its serious efforts and despite the support from the West, from Europe, that means that several other post-Soviet states will definitely be under threat,” he said, adding that Russia could pursue a “tough Soviet-like sphere of influence or even direct annexation” of these countries.

When was the last time a breakthrough appeared likely?

No talks have yet come close to a breakthrough.

Only perhaps at the end of March 2022, at the very start of the conflict, when the two countries met in Istanbul, there was some possibility of ending the conflict, said Olofsgard.

“At this point, the relative strengths of the two counterparts were not clear; Ukraine had proven stronger and Russia more incompetent than expected,” he said.

Ukraine was also more willing to make concessions with respect to joining NATO, not allowing foreign bases in Ukraine, and not demanding the immediate return of Crimea, Olofsgard added.

Ultimately, however, there were many factors contributing to the meeting’s failure in the end, “including the atrocities in Bucha, [a] lack of clear Western promises of security guarantees, Russian failures on the battlefield changing the calculations of both sides, and incompatible views on land concessions and military build-up of Ukraine”, he said.

Analysts talk about a guarantor to secure peace. They point out the example of American troops stationed in South Korea to this day following the 1953 Korean War armistice.

Ukraine would “probably need something like that”, Moshes said, adding that “no Western country has been seriously speaking about guaranteeing whatever the outcome of the negotiations might be”.

Why have repeated attempts to negotiate an end to this war failed?

Vast differences remain between the two sides.

While past meetings have facilitated important results, from prisoner exchanges to the return of kidnapped Ukrainian children from Russia, they have failed to address core differences, said Boyse, referring to territorial concessions and a security guarantee for Ukraine.

Ultimately, Russia wants to win the war – it wants a military victory over a diplomatic one, said Moshes.

“Russia is interested in continuing the war until Ukraine is defeated,” he said, adding that “Ukraine cannot accept capitulation after so many years of resistance [and] so much economic trouble”.

Boyse, the former US diplomat, said that Putin’s grand vision of reestablishing the Russian empire was the key obstacle.

“Putin has a colonial attitude towards Ukraine. He wants to control it or at a minimum, decide what goes on there,” said Boyse, adding that this was understandably unacceptable to Ukraine.

What would it take for these talks to produce a meaningful breakthrough?

Olexiy Haran, a Ukrainian professor of comparative politics at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, said some technical issues could be negotiated in Abu Dhabi this week, including grain supplies, a ceasefire in the Black Sea, an energy ceasefire and perhaps another exchange of prisoners.

But all the analysts were certain no peace accord would emerge from the talks.

“The White House has hinted at what appears to be some sort of a grand bargain that appears to expand the number of issues under negotiation to the European security order,” said Boyse.

But this assurance appears to focus primarily on meeting Russia’s demands, not Ukraine’s, he said.

“Russia is the demandeur and the aggressor and is pressing a weakened president who very much wants to be a peacemaker,” said the former US diplomat.

“Putin thinks he can win at the negotiation table what he cannot win on the battlefield.”

Olofsgard of the Stockholm Institute of Transition Economics said that Trump, who has become a lame-duck following his party’s losses in the midterm elections, may pay more attention to foreign policy during his remaining two years in power.

“This could imply that Trump will push even harder to make peace, or at least a ceasefire, in Ukraine. And given his past tendencies, that means leaning on Ukraine to make more concessions and trying to strike some kind of US business deals as a sweetener for Russia,” he said.

Analysts doubt a breakthrough would be achieved in the Abu Dhabi talks as the Russian leader would not offer major concessions.

“Putin’s way of negotiating is generally: demand the maximum, escalate, and wait until others compromise,” said Boyse.

articles.title: Iran stands by demands to end the war as US ramps up military pressure
articles.summary: Talks aimed at preventing new major fighting between the US and Iran are ongoing.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – The Iranian government has reported more strikes by the United States but insists this pressure will not impact its demands to end the war.

Ahmad Nafisi, deputy governor for Hormozgan, where the overnight US strikes hit, confirmed on Monday morning that the southern island of Qeshm was targeted but no residential and commercial areas or vital infrastructure were damaged.

The US did not directly acknowledge the air strikes, but Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated Washington’s characterisation of similar recent strikes on Qeshm as “defensive”. Previous attacks, the latest of which was acknowledged by President Donald Trump on Friday, have targeted Iranian air defences and radar installations.

Mediators are trying to prevent large-scale US attacks on Iran, which Trump has repeatedly threatened, with talks continuing. But Washington appears unwilling to accept Iran’s seven demands to end the war, which include the lifting of the US blockade on Iran’s southern ports and lifting sanctions on Tehran.

Esmail Baghaei, the spokesman of Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, on Monday rejected Rubio’s remarks that some of these seven demands were “ridiculous and really not realistic”.

“Iran’s plan is still the most logical plan on the table. I think it can lead to security returning to the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf, and create the grounds for a process,” Baghaei said during a news conference in Tehran.

The terms mostly amount to a return to the Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed in June between Iran and the US. But Tehran now has additional stipulations regarding the future of the Strait of Hormuz.

Baghaei said the US announcement of a reward of up to $20m for information on Iran’s nuclear programme is a ploy by the Trump administration to “convey the sense that the Iranian nuclear issue is still a threat”, after the Republican Party’s heavy defeats in midterm elections.

Tehran says it will not part with its highly enriched uranium, which is believed to be buried under the rubble of facilities bombed by the US and Israel last year. But it is open to downblending the material, which would be needed to build a nuclear bomb.

International inspectors have no access to Iranian nuclear sites, except for the Bushehr nuclear power plant, where the Foreign Ministry said there was a recent visit.

Iran has accused the International Atomic Energy Agency and its director, Rafael Grossi, of stepping out of their technical mandate and creating the grounds for attacks on nuclear facilities during last year’s 12-day war and the current war.

There have been signs of a positive breakthrough in mediation efforts, with reports that Trump and Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani will meet in the White House on Monday.

But Andreas Krieg, an associate professor at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that Washington’s biggest objection to the ongoing mediated talks is that Iran is essentially demanding the rewards of an agreement before providing the concessions to justify one.

“Reopening Hormuz within two days sounds accommodating, but it changes the timetable rather than the substance of the bargain,” he told Al Jazeera about the Iranian proposal.

Both the US and Iran’s Arab neighbours would not accept long-term Iranian-approved shipping corridors in the Strait of Hormuz.

Rubio and other officials are also against Iran’s demand for an end to hostilities across the region, as it would restrict Israel’s military freedom of action.

“Iran is going beyond a ceasefire, trying to translate its wartime leverage into a new regional security arrangement on its own terms,” Krieg said.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said Sunday that the country’s military mission in Iran remained unfinished, and threatened Lebanon’s Hezbollah with further territorial losses if it joined an Iranian attack.

Iranian authorities continue to warn ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz to refrain from taking “unauthorised” routes or face potential attacks.

Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesman Hossein Mohebbi rejected the claim by the US that all naval mines have been cleared from the Strait of Hormuz.

“Nobody dares enter the Strait of Hormuz to remove the mines,” he said on Sunday.

Iranian state television reported on Monday that 11 tankers have been attacked over the past 10 days, with four unable to continue transit.

IRGC-affiliated media cited an unnamed IRGC Navy source as claiming on Monday that maritime navigation systems were targeted in the southern areas of the waterway overnight, preventing tankers from transiting as part of the US-coordinated oil shuttle system .

Trump played down the prospects of a return to all-out war with Iran on Sunday, but added that the US military had marked civilian infrastructure like 38 bridges as targets if the war restarts at scale.

Krieg said he expects Tehran to continue its strategy of “controlled escalation” rather than immediate all-out retaliation against the US strikes.

“The new American effort to disrupt Iran’s overland trade will reinforce this strategy. Tehran will increasingly seek to make the Gulf states bear the economic consequences of Washington’s decisions, hoping they will pressure Trump towards compromise,” Krieg said.

“Washington may believe it is conducting a limited campaign of coercion, while Tehran increasingly sees an unrestricted economic war against its survival. At some point, Iran may decide that the costs of continued restraint exceed the risks of escalation.”

articles.title: UK court hands comedian Russell Brand 10.5 years for rape, sexual assault
articles.summary: Brand was convicted last week of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three more between 2004 and 2009.
articles.body:
A British court has sentenced comedian and actor Russell Brand to 10 years and six months in prison for rape and sexual assault.

London’s Southwark Crown Court handed down the sentence on Monday. Brand was convicted last week of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three more between 2004 and 2009.

The British media personality, known for outrageous stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, asserted that he was innocent and that all his encounters were consensual.

However, a jury of eight men and four women on Thursday convicted him of attacks on four of six accusers. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

His victims delivered powerful statements during the sentencing hearing, describing the trauma his attacks had caused.

Brand was a sexual predator who believed “fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live”, Judge Joel Bennathan said at the sentencing hearing.

He showed “casual and arrogant disregard” for women, Bennathan added.

“About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous,” he said. “You were clever — and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator.”

The 51-year-old Brand, who had sought during the trial to present himself as a newly devout Christian, showed little emotion during the hearing. He has denied ever having non-consensual sex.

His lawyer Ian Winter said Brand “is a fundamentally different person today and has been for a very long time”, and has now recovered from his addiction to drugs and alcohol.

One victim, whom Brand raped in 2009, said in a statement read by prosecutors that the trauma of the ⁠attack was “something I carry with me every day and it often feels never-ending”.

London’s Metropolitan Police said Brand is under investigation for two other alleged rapes, one involving ‌a then-16-year-old girl, and the head of the force said on Friday that he “wouldn’t be surprised if many more came forward”.

articles.title: Cruise ship pianist rescued by fishermen after nine hours treading water in Pacific Ocean
articles.summary: Two fishermen have rescued a man thought to have been treading water off the coast of California for nine hours after falling from a cruise ship.
articles.body: Two fishermen have rescued a man thought to have been treading water off the coast of California for nine hours after falling from a cruise ship. Grant Garrett and Sean Norton told CNN affiliate KCBS/KCAL that they were around 20 miles from shore when they came across the man in the water on Friday morning. “I’m like, ‘Yeah, it’s a human being. Stop the boat; let’s get all of our lines in,’” Garrett said. Norton added that the episode was “surreal.” “Grant and I each got an arm and lifted him up,” Norton said. “He was in total shock.” “The only thing he said to me was, ‘Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,’” Norton said. He later told them he was a pianist on a Royal Caribbean cruise ship named “Ovation of the Seas,” and Newport County officials believe the man went overboard about nine hours before he was found, KCBS/KCAL reported. The man is expected to survive, but Norton said he believes he might not have done so without the El Niño weather phenomenon, which is associated with higher water temperatures in the Pacific Ocean. “You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water’s 76 degrees,” Norton said. “A different year, no way he makes it.” A spokesperson for Royal Caribbean told CNN: “We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share.” CNN has contacted the US Coast Guard and Newport County lifeguards for comment.

articles.body: Snoop Dogg founded the Snoop Youth Football League in 2005 to give children from inner-city communities the chance to take part in football and cheerleading. The non-profit organisation serves children aged 5 to 13, with an emphasis on teamwork, discipline, sportsmanship and academics.Its first season took place in the Los Angeles area in autumn 2005, when more than 1,300 children participated. According to the Snoop Football League (2024), more than 60,000 children have taken part over its first 18 years.The league also gives young players opportunities to travel and compete in other cities. It aims to bring communities together through sport while teaching children character, integrity, fair play and healthy competition through its football and cheer programmes.Snoop Dogg’s youth football league began in 2005 with more than 1,300 childrenThe Snoop Youth Football League was founded by Snoop Dogg, and its inaugural season was held in autumn 2005. More than 1,300 children took part in that first season in the Los Angeles area. The programme began in September and included seven regular-season games, followed by a three-week playoff. The season ended with a championship event known as the ‘Super Bowl’ in late November.The league also selected all-star teams, whose players travelled to Houston to compete. An all-star team is chosen each year to visit another city and play against children from other football leagues. These trips form part of the opportunities described by the organisation for participating young players during its opening year.What does Snoop Dogg’s youth football league aim to teach childrenThe league describes itself as a non-profit organisation established to give children from inner-city communities the opportunity to participate in youth football and cheer. It serves children between 5 and 13 years old. Alongside participation in sport, the programme teaches values including teamwork, good sportsmanship, discipline and self-respect. The organisation also stresses the importance of academics.Its stated objective is to make participation possible regardless of a child's race, colour, creed or economic background. Through football and cheer, it seeks to help young people learn character, integrity, discipline and teamwork. It also wants to bring communities together through a shared interest in sport and encourage fair play and fellowship among participants for young people in participating communities.How does Snoop Dogg’s youth football league give children opportunities to travelThe league's first season included opportunities beyond its games in Los Angeles. It selected all-star teams and sent participants to Houston, where they competed with children from other football leagues. An all-star team is selected each year to travel to another city for similar competition. The organisation describes these trips as a chance for children to travel by aeroplane, visit states they may never have imagined going to and play in some of the country's most prestigious stadiums.Community support remains central to Snoop Dogg’s youth football leagueAccording to Snoop Youth Football League, its objective extends beyond teaching children how to play football or cheer. It aims to promote character, integrity, discipline and teamwork, while bringing people from different communities together through sport. The organisation also identifies fair play and fellowship as part of its purpose.Its stated objectives include teaching the elements of the games in ways that promote safety, enjoyment and healthy competition. The league invites people to support its work through financial contributions, equipment donations and volunteering. It also encourages people to attend its games. articles.title: Tommy Walsh: Ground Force and Homes Under the Hammer star dies aged 69
articles.summary: The building and DIY expert also appeared on TV shows like Challenge Tommy Walsh and Clean It, Fix It.
articles.body:
Tommy Walsh, the building and DIY expert known for starring on TV shows including Ground Force, Homes Under the Hammer and Challenge Tommy Walsh, has died at the age of 69.

Walsh started his career as a professional builder before rising to fame alongside Alan Titchmarsh and Charlie Dimmock on the BBC's Ground Force from 1997 to 2005.

He went on to also front popular programmes including Clean It, Fix It, and Cowboys and Angels, and joined daytime TV favourite Homes Under the Hammer in 2021.

Walsh's agent told BBC News he died "peacefully after a long illness surrounded by his family", and asked for privacy for the family.

Walsh was previously reported to have had surgery for throat cancer in 2022 and lung cancer in 2023.

Walsh got his big break on TV after restoring the house of a BBC producer who was working on ideas for a show that would turn into Ground Force.

"She asked me to look at a couple of pilots. One of them was the precursor to Ground Force, called Over the Garden Wall," he told the BBC in 2004 . "It was like watching paint dry - it was terrible."

Walsh said he initially turned down the chance to star on the show three times - but agreed when his eight-year-old daughter told him she had made a £10 bet with a boy at school that her dad was going to be on TV.

He found a winning formula with his co-stars, who performed makeovers on gardens belonging to members of the public.

His other shows included Tommy Walsh's Eco House, Tommy's DIY Survival, Trading Places, Space Invaders and Fix Your House For Free; and he published a number of DIY books.

articles.title: Blue state repeat offender accused of murdering wife at family’s home months after domestic violence charge
articles.summary: Thomas John Iovenitti was out on just $1,000 bail for domestic violence charges when he allegedly stabbed his wife Alisha in their Concord home.

The repeat offender, Thomas John Iovenitti, 40, of Concord is accused of murdering his wife, Alisha Iovenitti, 39, in the family's home last month. articles.title: Luton-based EasyJet looking to axe 50 head office jobs
articles.summary: It is understood the proposals are to cut up to 50 head office roles out of a 2,300-strong team.
articles.body:
EasyJet has confirmed plans to cut head office jobs ahead of its £5.7bn private equity takeover.

The low-cost Luton-based carrier is understood to be consulting on proposals that could see up to about 50 head office roles axed out of a 2,300-strong team.

It came after EasyJet agreed in July to a takeover for 715p a share by US firm Apollo , which also owns Wagamama's parent company The Restaurant Group.

Shareholders are voting on the deal on Wednesday and, if approved, it is expected to complete in the first quarter of 2027. It is understood that the job cuts are not linked to Apollo or the takeover.

An EasyJet spokesperson said: "Our people are integral to EasyJet's success, and as a low-cost airline, we always operate efficiently so we can keep fares low for our customers and invest in future growth opportunities.

"These proposals affect a very small proportion of head office roles to ensure we are best set up to support the business' ambitious plans."

Unions in the UK and Europe have voiced concerns over possible job cuts after the Apollo deal as well as debts that would be put onto the airline's balance sheet.

Apollo previously said it wants to help the airline grow and that it does not intend to cut any jobs in the first 12 months after the takeover has been completed, implying that passengers can expect largely the same service.

But the British Airline Pilots Association (BALPA) trade union said recently that "important questions remain regarding the long-term implications of the transaction".

The union added that its principal concern was "the extent to which the transaction may affect employees beyond the 12-month period covered by the statements of intention."

EasyJet was founded by Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou in 1995 to offer a low-cost alternative to British Airways, and it has since expanded to be one of the largest networks across Europe.

Sir Stelios and his family, who own about 15% of the business, have given the takeover their support.

Apollo secured the deal after winning in a takeover tussle with US investment firm Castlelake.

Castlelake had previously made a £5.5bn, or 690p a share, proposal to buy EasyJet, but walked away from the bidding war in August.

articles.title: Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assaults
articles.summary: The judge told the British celebrity that he had shown a "casual and arrogant disregard" to any woman's right to say "no" to him.
articles.body:
The British former comedian and actor Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three more.

Handing down the sentence Monday at Southwark Crown Court in London, judge Joel Bennathan said Brand told a series of lies throughout the trial, adding he had displayed a "casual and arrogant disregard" for women who said 'No' to him.

"About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous," Bennathan said. "You were clever — and in many people's eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator."

He added, "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say 'no' and to demand justice from criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent."

Brand was supported in court by his wife, Laura Gallacher, and his father, Ron. He is expected to serve at least two-thirds of that sentence — around seven years — before being eligible for release.

Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Nov. 5. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones called Brand a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator" who treated women as a "disposable commodity."

"Mr. Brand abused the influence and power that came with his fame," Karmy-Jones said. "He used it to facilitate an access to women without which the offending could not have taken place. It also fed his own view that he could commit such offenses with impunity."

Ahead of his sentencing, one woman, who was sexually assaulted by Brand in 2004 or 2005, told the court Monday in her impact statement: "Russell Brand is a sexual predator who has no remorse," Sky News reported.

Another woman, who was raped by the comedian in 2009 after meeting him at a comedy show in London, said she was "living with trauma." She said his fame made it "difficult to escape reminders of what had happened," Reuters reported.

She said she was worried after the attack that she might have HIV, struggled to eat and sleep, took two to three months off work and abandoned the career she had embarked upon. "Although the rape was 17 years ago, she still finds it affects her ability to form new friendships and to know when she can trust people," the judge said.

A third woman who was assaulted by Brand while working on a Channel 4 documentary said that, following the attack, she felt like she had "lost my trust in people." Reflecting on the incident, she added: "I felt powerless in that moment."

Last week, Megyn Kelly, the former Fox News host, reacted to Brand's conviction in disbelief.

"I don't believe the charges, and I don't have to believe them just because a jury came through with the opposite conclusion," she said in a YouTube livestream .

The next day, in a comment on X, Elon Musk described Brand's conviction for offenses nearly 20 years old as a " crazy legal standard ." England doesn't have a statute of limitations for rape or sexual assault.

Brand became a household name in the U.K. in the 2000s as a comedian and broadcaster and had well-documented issues with drugs and alcohol. He went on to star in the movies Get Him to the Greek in 2010 and Arthur the following year.

He married singer Katy Perry in October 2010, but Brand filed for divorce in December 2011, citing irreconcilable differences. Their divorce was finalized in July 2012.

The claims against Brand were made by six different women, spanning from 1999 to 2009. None of the women knew each other, but came forward to police following a TV documentary and press reports in 2023, in which anonymous allegations were made by other women.

During the trial, the court heard tearful testimony from the six accusers, who are all entitled to lifelong anonymity.

According to the Associated Press, the convictions included a rape that took place in 2009, involving a woman who went to Brand's home after meeting him at one of his shows. She said she had engaged in consensual sex, but that Brand then raped her and removed a condom in the process.

Brand was also convicted of sexually assaulting a woman when he grabbed her breasts at a London bar in 2004.

He was also found guilty over an incident in 2009, in which he demanded a woman give him a massage in front of two of his colleagues and then put his head in her groin.

A third complaint of sexual assault ended in a guilty verdict when Brand was found guilty of pushing a woman who worked at a radio station up against a wall and forcibly kissing her.

Brand denied the charges and said he had never forced anyone to do something against their will.

Footage released by London's Metropolitan Police after the verdict shows Brand being interviewed by police in December 2023.

"As I've repeatedly stated publicly and written about extensively, I led a very promiscuous life in the past, which I've spent years openly denouncing," Brand can be seen saying. "I've never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity."

He said he did "not recall the names" of the complainants, or meeting them, adding, "However, it's entirely possible that I may have encountered them and we may have engaged in consensual sexual activity or physical contact that's been since reimagined."

Following the verdict, London's Metropolitan Police Service told Yahoo News that Brand, 51, was facing further allegations of rape from two women.

"The suspect has previously been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations," the force said. Brand has not been charged in relation to these claims.

The head of the Met Police, Sir Mark Rowley, has urged any other victims of Brand to contact the police. "There's two more rape allegations that we're looking at. We're encouraging anybody else to come forward if there's any other allegations," he told British media on Nov. 6.

He later said that he "wouldn't be surprised if many, many more come forward," adding of the trial, "This shows that powerful people can be brought down so you are safe stepping forward and we will support and try and bring that person to justice."

articles.title: Welch doubles down on TPUSA feud, calls group 'losers' after laughing at joke about killing Charlie Kirk again
articles.summary: Jennifer Welch fired back at Turning Point USA in a new video, calling them "losers" and insisting her apology over the Charlie Kirk joke wasn't for them.
articles.body: Liberal podcaster Jennifer Welch escalated her feud with the organization, Turning Point USA (TPUSA), calling the group "losers" and saying an apology for laughing about killing TPUSA founder Charlie Kirk again wasn't meant for conservatives. Welch and her "I’ve Had It Podcast" co-host, Angie Sullivan, issued a mealy-mouthed apology on Saturday, saying they shouldn’t have laughed at an "insensitive joke" and noting they would donate to a gun violence prevention organization. "There's a huge online cancellation campaign from all the titty babies over at Turning Point that want ‘I’ve Had It Podcast’ to be canceled," Welch said in a video and posted to Instagram on Sunday. "Why is Turning Point spearheading this? Well, let me tell you why. They are in big trouble," Welch continued. "Even Republicans are starting to question, ‘Are they worth it?’ They get millions of dollars in funding, and as everybody saw on Tuesday, they got L after L after L, because they’re losers and they lost." ERIKA KIRK CHANNELS CHARLIE WITH BLUNT MESSAGE TO CONSERVATIVES AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES Welch insisted they "believe in nothing," and are "trying to ignite a war" with her far-left podcast. "They want to prove to their donors, ‘We can cancel libs,'" Welch said. Welch then turned her attention to Kolvet, who said the liberal podcasters are "part of a toxic and evil culture that perpetuates violence against conservatives." Welch and Sullivan drew sharp backlash last week after they broke out into laughter while reading a post aloud: "We're digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again." Kolvet had previously responded to the apology that Welch and Sullivan issued once sponsors began to flee their show, suggesting he wouldn’t listen until they actually changed their ways. But the "I’ve Had It Podcast" co-hosts don’t appear willing to budge. "Andrew, we’re never, ever, going to sit down and listen to you," Welch said. HERE’S WHAT THE WORLD NEVER UNDERSTOOD "When we apologize for laughing at a joke on our podcast, that wasn’t for you, that was for us, because somebody that I love very much died from gun violence… and I just didn’t feel good about that," she continued. "That apology was, so that when I advocate commonsense gun reform, that I’m doing it clean and clear. I don’t expect you to understand this, because at Turning Point, you all laugh at violence all the time." Welch continued criticizing Kolvet, saying the notion that he thought the apology was for him "exemplifies how out of whack you are with where the American people are right now." "This is their pathetic attempt to cancel us," Welch said. "Let’s grow this thing and show Turning Point how irrelevant they are." Welch also called Turning Point a "hateful organization," before Sullivan chimed in with a vulgar outburst. Kolvet responded to their video by posting, "Dear Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan, Thanks for the video, but it’s not that hard. Just don’t legitimize political violence. You can blame me or Turning Point all you want, but we’re not the reason all your sponsors are fleeing. You are. Your lack of remorse is the least surprising thing of all. I never once expected you to listen to me. But maybe, just maybe, you’ll listen to all the brands that no longer want to be associated with you." HOW CHARLIE KIRK’S ASSASSINATION CHANGED THE WAY CONSERVATIVES APPROACH HOSTILE OPPONENTS Fox News Digital reached out to Kolvet for additional comment but did not immediately hear back. Welch was an Oklahoma City-based interior designer who starred in the short-lived Bravo reality show "Sweet Home Oklahoma" from 2017-2018. In 2022, she launched "I've Had It" with Sullivan and the program has since emerged as one of the most popular anti-Trump platforms in media. When reached for comment, Welch didn’t appear too concerned about advertisers distancing themselves from her podcast. "We laughed at an insensitive joke. We regret it, and we apologized. We removed the segment from the episode because we oppose gun violence in all of its forms and made a donation to Everytown for Gun Safety to put our money where our mouth is. Turning Point, the group leading the cancellation against us, mocks violence and never apologizes," Welch told Fox News Digital. "We still have plenty of advertisers and we aren't going anywhere," she continued. "Each and every day we will relentlessly fight for equality and justice for every American, and we enthusiastically welcome the nearly 30,000 new followers that have come to our channel in the last few days." articles.title: Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta closes citing gov’t clampdown
articles.summary: The paper was one of the few remaining outlets in Russia that criticised Moscow’s war on Ukraine.
articles.body:
Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta has ended operations due to pressure from authorities.

The newspaper reported that it held its last editorial meeting on Monday and closed its newsroom. It announced last month that it was being forced to shut down after being classed as a “foreign agent” by Moscow, a label used to stifle dissent.

The Russian media has come under increased scrutiny from the state amid Moscow’s war on Ukraine. In October, authorities searched the home of Novaya Gazeta’s editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, and took him in for questioning. Another editor at the paper, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested in April.

Cofounder Dmitry Muratov addressed journalists who gathered to witness the closure of the Novaya Gazeta office in Moscow.

“Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today,” he said, adding that constitutional guarantees for political and civil rights had “effectively ceased to function”.

Novaya Gazeta was one of the few remaining outlets that openly criticised Russia’s war on Ukraine and the Kremlin’s policies, amid a widening crackdown on the media and free speech.

In September, the outlet was designated a “foreign agent”. Novaya Gazeta said that since then banks had stopped processing the reader donations on which it relied for financial survival.

United Nations human rights chief Volker Turk said in October that Novaya Gazeta’s closure was “yet another devastating blow for remaining independent media” in Russia.

The Kremlin played down the closure, saying it was part of “a normal cycle of change”.

The paper was co-founded by former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev and funded with money from his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize. It continued reporting despite censorship tightening in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Several of its reporters have been murdered in killings widely seen as retribution for their work, among them Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating abuses by Russia’s military in Chechnya and criticised President Vladimir Putin’s rule.

She was found dead in her apartment block in 2006.

articles.title: Steel plant blast kills 16 in western Turkey
articles.summary: A blast at a steel and iron manufacturing plant in western Turkey on Monday killed 16 people, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said after a cabinet meeting.
articles.body: A blast at a steel and iron manufacturing plant in western Turkey on Monday killed 16 people, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said after a cabinet meeting. An explosion took place at around noon (4 a.m. ET) at the Habas iron and steel manufacturing plant in the Aliaga district of coastal Izmir province, the governor’s office said in a statement. According to initial findings, the incident occurred when a ceiling crane snapped and fell into an arc furnace during the liquid steel casting process. Footage broadcast by local TV stations showed large plumes of gray dust rising above the plant. Those injured were rushed to various hospitals in the region for treatment. Three of the 14 injured were in serious condition, according to the statement. Search and rescue operations were ongoing to reach 10 people still trapped under the rubble after the blast.

articles.title: Ukraine peace talks to restart after 9 months. What makes them different this time?
articles.summary: A fresh round of peace talks between the US, Ukraine and Russia are set to begin Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, as the Trump administration renews its drive to end the nearly five-year conflict even after it announced significant concessions to Moscow.
articles.body: A fresh round of peace talks between the US, Ukraine and Russia are set to begin Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, as the Trump administration renews its drive to end the nearly five-year conflict even after it announced significant concessions to Moscow. Russia has made clear it wants the negotiations – the first of their kind since February – to be strictly trilateral, though national security advisers from several European nations, as well as officials from NATO and the European Union, are also expected in the UAE capital for separate meetings. “We are working hard to find a negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine,” US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and US negotiator Jared Kushner said Monday. US officials on Monday underlined that posture, saying that the upcoming talks are a new starting point in defining an end to the war, including discussions on security guarantees and a “post-war security architecture.” “We need to come up with a way that, when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war, and we believe that’s what Ukraine wants. We believe that’s what Europe wants and we believe that’s what Russia wants,” one official said. However, many – particularly in Europe – have cast doubt on Moscow’s intentions. The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said Monday she saw little sign that Russia was willing to negotiate in good faith. Meanwhile, the US official also said that it would be up to Trump to decide whether to offer a US security guarantee as part of peace talks. Who is leading the negotiations? The US will be represented by Kushner and Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff, while Ukraine’s foreign intelligence chief and top negotiator Rustem Umerov will lead the Ukrainian delegation, according to the official with knowledge of the talks. Russia is sending deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin as delegates, according to Russian state news agency TASS, as well as Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and member of general staff Yuri Zhigarlovsky. Representatives from the E4 group – the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Italy – as well as officials from NATO and the European Commission will also be in Abu Dhabi, Umerov said Monday. “We will hold separate coordination meetings with our European partners,” Umerov added. Asked about the presence of European officials in Abu Dhabi, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that Europe has its own channels of communication with Kyiv and Washington, while reaffirming that the talks are “a trilateral negotiation – involving Russia and Ukraine – with the United States acting as a mediator.” What makes these talks different? Notably, these talks come amid a renewed push by European nations for a more active role in negotiations over Ukraine’s future, and the security of the bloc at large, after Trump touted a new security deal for Ukraine that “might involve all of Europe.” “The Europeans will be well represented,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told French media Sunday. “In recent weeks, the Europeans have made their voices heard. They have expressed to the American mediator that no discussion affecting the future of the continent can ignore our expectations and demands,” he added. Europe has long been wary of any US-brokered peace deal negotiated without its involvement, with Umerov saying Monday that Ukraine was “doing everything we can to ensure that Europe is a participant in the diplomatic process.” While the talks will remain trilateral, Kushner said that he and Witkoff would also meet with European partners to continue the “close consultation and coordination we have undertaken on European security and Ukraine’s postwar future over the past several weeks.” “Ultimately, achieving a comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them,” Kushner posted on X. How likely is a breakthrough? This will be the fourth round of trilateral talks. All have ended without significant breakthrough. Earlier this year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the most recent trilateral talks in Geneva, Switzerland, in February fell short of Ukraine’s goals, saying “sensitive political matters, issues of possible compromises and the necessary meeting of leaders have not yet been sufficiently worked through.” The US later postponed a round of trilateral talks that were expected to take place in March due to the war in Iran. Putin is still making maximalist demands previously rejected by Kyiv, including Russian control over Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, a reduction in the size of Ukraine’s military and the abandonment of Kyiv’s ambitions to join NATO. John Herbst, senior director of the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center and a former US ambassador to Ukraine, said any expectations for the Abu Dhabi talks should be “very modest.” “They are only taking place because Putin wants to give Trump a reason to continue to distance himself from Ukraine,” Herbst wrote last week. What is the situation on the ground in Ukraine? With Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year and gains on the battlefield remaining difficult to come by, Moscow has escalated its aerial attacks – with deadly results for Ukrainians. At least 55 people were killed last Monday when Russia dropped several bombs on a school building used as a shelter and aid center in Zaporizhzhia, marking one of the deadliest single incidents of the war to date. Civilian deaths in Ukraine are at their highest point since the start of the war, with more than 2,700 killed in Russian strikes so far this year, according to ACLED, a global conflict monitor. And continuing a pattern seen in previous years, Russian drones and missiles are already hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, but harder and earlier than in other winters, analysts say. Russian attacks on the power grid left more than 600,000 people in the Dnipropetrovsk region without electricity overnight into Sunday, Zelensky said, as temperatures plummet and winter draws in. Over the past few months, Russia has deployed faster, jet-powered Shahed drones, which are harder to shoot down. At the same time, more missiles are slipping through Ukraine’s air defenses as Kyiv grapples with a chronic shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors that are one of the few defensive weapons capable of shooting down ballistic missiles. Where does the US stand on the war – and could the midterms change that? Where the Biden administration positioned the US as Ukraine’s biggest single donor and most powerful ally, the Trump administration’s relationship with Kyiv has been decidedly more complicated. It halted financial aid to Ukraine at the beginning of 2025, while the intelligence and technology support it still provides has come under strain in recent weeks too. Last month, Zelensky accused his Western allies of not providing intelligence warnings before multiple ballistic missile attacks, a claim that the Trump administration denied. In October too, Ukraine’s ability to use Starshield, a military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink service that is critical to its military operations, was hampered when speed limits were imposed on the satellite terminals. Trump denied approving that decision, while Musk said the Trump administration was behind the ban in a social media post. Undergirding all this recent tension has been Trump’s sensitivity to rising gas prices, which skyrocketed due to the Iran war and contributed to the Republicans’ landslide defeat in last week’s midterms. He has shown a willingness to strike business deals with Moscow, including one to supply markets with Russia’s diesel, in a sharp break from the sanctions aimed at punishing and isolating the Russian economy, and pressured Zelensky to accept a short-lived “energy ceasefire.” So, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, Zelensky has publicly said he hopes the “blue wave” can bolster US support for Ukraine since the party “speaks very clearly about supporting Ukraine and providing assistance to Ukraine.” It remains unclear whether the midterms will substantively change US policy toward Kyiv, however. In a “60 Minutes” interview that aired Sunday, Trump refused to say whether he trusted Zelensky or Putin more and suggested Ukraine may have to cede some of its territory. “They’re gonna end up with a little bit different shape, Ukraine,” he said, outlining a scenario that Zelensky has repeatedly rejected. CNN’s Kit Maher, Charlotte Reck, Ivana Kottasová, Tim Lister, Matthew Chance, Victoria Butenko and Lauren Kent contributed reporting.

articles.title: Prince Harry steps down as BetterUp chief impact officer after five years on reported $1 million salary; Duke takes senior adviser role following UK return with Meghan Markle and children
articles.summary: Prince Harry has stepped down from his high-profile position as chief impact officer at US-based mental health and coaching company BetterUp, five years
articles.body: Prince Harry has stepped down from his high-profile position as chief impact officer at US-based mental health and coaching company BetterUp, five years after joining the Silicon Valley firm. The Duke of Sussex will now serve as a senior adviser, marking a significant change in his professional responsibilities following his reported return to the UK with Meghan Markle and their children in August 2026.The development was announced by BetterUp CEO and co-founder Alexi Robichaux on November 6. While Harry is stepping away from the company's leadership team, he will continue to remain associated with the organisation in an advisory capacity.The announcement comes less than three months after the Sussexes' reported relocation to Britain, bringing fresh attention to the Duke's professional commitments outside the royal family.Why Prince Harry stepped down from the leadership positionAccording to Robichaux, the transition is intended to give Harry greater flexibility to focus on other professional and personal commitments. In his announcement, the BetterUp CEO said the Duke would work on selected projects involving some of the company's biggest corporate clients.He will also have more time to expand his investment portfolio, explore new business opportunities and continue supporting philanthropic initiatives.Robichaux thanked Harry for his contribution over the past five years and praised his understanding of coaching and mental fitness. He also reiterated that the company's partnership with the Invictus Games Foundation, founded by Harry, would continue.Prince Harry joined BetterUp in 2021 after stepping back from royal dutiesHarry joined BetterUp in March 2021, becoming the company's first chief impact officer. It was among his first major corporate appointments after he and Meghan stepped back from their roles as senior working royals and relocated to the United States.At the time, his responsibilities included advocating for mental fitness, raising awareness about mental health and helping guide the company's social mission.Harry had also spoken about his personal experience with coaching, describing how working with a coach had given him valuable advice and a fresh perspective. He had expressed his intention to use the position to create a positive impact on people's lives.The Duke's reported annual remuneration of around $1 million had attracted attention when he joined the company. However, neither BetterUp's latest announcement nor its CEO has disclosed his revised compensation under the senior adviser arrangement. The reported figure should therefore not be treated as his confirmed current salary.Harry makes low-key Remembrance Sunday appearance in the UKThe change in his professional role comes amid renewed attention on Harry's return to Britain. On November 8, the Duke made an unannounced appearance at a Remembrance Sunday memorial service in Brackley, Northamptonshire.Harry was seen standing among local residents, wearing his military medals and a red poppy. He attended the local commemoration while King Charles III, Prince William, Queen Camilla and other senior members of the Royal Family participated in the national ceremony at London's Cenotaph.An onlooker told SWNS that Harry remained at the service throughout and later went into the market to greet residents. His appearance marked his first Remembrance Sunday since returning to live in the UK.What lies ahead for Prince Harry?Although Harry is relinquishing his executive position, his association with BetterUp is not ending. His new advisory role will allow him to remain involved in selected corporate projects while pursuing other investments, business ventures and charitable commitments.For now, BetterUp has described the transition as a continuation of its relationship with the Duke rather than a complete departure. articles.title: Jennifer Garner ran one mile every day for 67 days to support malnourished children; her Save the Children campaign raised $500,000 towards a $1 million goal
articles.summary: Actress Jennifer Garner turned a personal fitness challenge into a fundraising effort for children facing severe malnutrition, running one mile every day
articles.body: Actress Jennifer Garner turned a personal fitness challenge into a fundraising effort for children facing severe malnutrition, running one mile every day for 67 consecutive days in 2025. Through Save the Children’s #67Strong4Kids campaign, she aimed to draw attention to a condition that remains a major threat to young lives despite being preventable and treatable. The initiative combined physical activity with a simple fundraising message, linking the distance she covered to the cost of providing lifesaving nutritional treatment. By the end of the challenge, the campaign had collected $500,000 towards its $1 million fundraising goal.How Jennifer Garner’s 67-mile challenge supported malnourished childrenAccording to Save the Children’s press release, Garner launched the #67Strong4Kids challenge on her birthday in April, committing herself to running one mile daily for 67 days. The campaign was designed around the $67 required to provide a severely malnourished child with a complete six-week course of ready-to-use therapeutic food, commonly known as RUTF.The idea gave the challenge a clear purpose beyond exercise. Each mile represented an opportunity to raise awareness about childhood hunger and encourage people to contribute towards treatment that could help children recover from severe malnutrition.Why the campaign focused on severe acute malnutritionThe need behind the initiative was highlighted in Save the Children’s announcement. The organisation reported that one in five deaths among children under 5 was associated with severe acute malnutrition, a condition that can affect physical growth, cognitive development and a child's ability to resist illness.The condition is preventable and treatable, but children experiencing it need timely access to nutritional support. Save the Children explained that RUTF provides a practical way to deliver treatment to severely malnourished children.A contribution of $67 could fund a six-week treatment course, giving supporters a clearer understanding of how their money could help. Global Heroes noted that climate disruptions, conflict and economic instability contribute to the wider hunger crisis, leaving children exposed to conditions that threaten their survival.Becs Gentry and supporters joined Garner for the final mileThe challenge reached its finish line on June 22, 2025, with a public running event in Santa Monica, California. Save the Children reported that hundreds of people joined Garner and elite runner Becs Gentry, either in person or virtually, to complete the final mile.The event was sponsored by Brooks Running and marked the end of Garner's personal 67-day commitment. It also provided an opportunity to bring more people into the campaign and encourage continued fundraising after her individual challenge had finished.According to Save the Children, Gentry had been supporting the organisation since childhood and was inspired to take part in the initiative. She joined Garner for the final run, helping turn the personal challenge into a collective effort.How the $500,000 fundraising milestone was reachedBy June 22, the #67Strong4Kids campaign had raised $500,000, according to Save the Children. The amount represented half of the initiative's $1 million fundraising target, prompting the organisation and Garner to encourage supporters to continue contributing.Global Heroes reported that the campaign attracted people who took on their own 67-day challenges. Participants were not limited to running, with activities such as cycling, dancing, drawing and meditation also used to raise awareness and encourage donations.The campaign was designed to be accessible to people with different interests and abilities. Save the Children explained that people could set up a fundraiser in around 10 minutes. The initiative encouraged participants to choose an activity they enjoyed and commit to it for 67 days, although even a single day of participation was welcomed.Jennifer Garner's longstanding connection with Save the ChildrenGarner's involvement in #67Strong4Kids was part of a longer relationship with Save the Children. She is an actress and trustee who had supported the organisation for more than a decade.She travelled to several US states to meet lawmakers, journalists and philanthropists as part of her efforts to promote the organisation's work.Global Heroes highlighted other initiatives associated with Garner, including #SaveWithStories during the pandemic and a partnership involving Once Upon a Farm, the organic children's food company she co-founded.Although Garner completed her daily running commitment in June 2025, the fundraising effort was not intended to end with the final mile. Save the Children's campaign page continued encouraging people to donate or establish their own challenges to help reach the $1 million target.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Explosion at Turkish steel plant kills at least 16 people
articles.summary: President Erdogan announces an investigation after a crane collapsed into a furnace, triggering the blast near Izmir.
articles.body:
An explosion at a steel plant in western Turkiye has killed at least 16 people and injured 13 others.

The blast happened at 11:46am local time (08:46 GMT) on Monday at the HABAS factory in Aliaga, about 60km (37 miles) north of Izmir, which sits on the Aegean Sea in western Turkiye.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has announced an investigation and reported that two of the wounded were in serious condition.

Izmir’s governor said the explosion was caused by an overhead crane falling into a large industrial furnace while the boiler was being replaced.

Izmir Mayor Cemil Tugay said that the full number of dead and injured would only become clear once the rubble had been cleared.

Deniz Ulker, an eyewitness, said the explosion felt like an “earthquake”.

“When I looked at the factory across the street, thick black smoke was coming out. A fire broke out where the chimney was,” he said.

Workers’ groups say there is a long record of safety issues at the factory.

The Izmir chapter of Turkiye’s Labour Party, a small Marxist group, said it was “the third fatal incident” at the factory in three weeks.

Writing on X, it warned that seven employees had died in accidents at the plant in the past 10 years and said that maintenance requirements and safety standards were not being met.

The European Union and Azerbaijan were among those to send condolences.

articles.title: Now, Cong-led Keralam govt follows Karnataka on 'ethanol test'
articles.summary: BENGALURU/NEW DELHI/T'PURAM: Following in Congress-governed Karnataka's footsteps, the Congress-led govt of Keralam Monday started collecting petrol
articles.body: BENGALURU/NEW DELHI/T'PURAM: Following in Congress-governed Karnataka's footsteps, the Congress-led govt of Keralam Monday started collecting petrol samples to test whether their ethanol content was more than the prescribed 20%, setting up a likely Centre-state confrontation over E20 fuel.Keralam civil supplies minister Anoop Jacob said officials collected six samples each from nine petrol pumps across Thiruvananthapuram, Ernakulam, Kozhikode and Kannur, in the presence of OMC representatives.PESO-approved bottles and trained officials were used, he said, adding that further rounds of testing would follow and prosecution would be initiated if excess blending was detected.This prompted Union minister of state for petroleum Suresh Gopi to say that states were free to conduct tests but they should avoid political mudslinging. "Let them conduct the tests, whether it is Karnataka or Keralam govt. We have scientific support for it," he said. The minister warned that those creating controversies for political purposes would have to face consequences. Gopi said Centre had permitted 20% blending after assessing scientific feasibility and was implementing the transition gradually.On Monday, Karnataka defended its third-party laboratory findings about ethanol levels of up to 31.2%, rejecting a joint rebuttal by three oil marketing companies - IOCL, BPCL and HPCL. State food and civil supplies minister Rizwan Arshad termed objections raised by the three OMCs "illogical" and accused them of trying to push for a fresh joint survey after recalibrating the ethanol mix.He said state govt would send its findings to Centre, seek changes in testing protocols and demand discounted prices for E20 petrol, stressing that higher ethanol content reduced mileage and raised the effective cost for consumers.Arshad said alleged blending of up to 30% was happening at six terminals where ethanol was mixed with petrol before distribution, not at retail outlets. Karnataka said authorised officials followed prescribed sampling procedures, with labels jointly signed by officials and dealers. After OMC laboratories failed to provide ethanol percentages for the initial 63 samples, the state sent them to NABL-accredited, ISO-certified third-party laboratories.The three OMCs had challenged Karnataka's Oct tests, questioning its sampling and laboratory methodology. articles.title: SC ban goes up in smoke as crackers burst past deadlines until sunrise in Noida, Ghaziabad
articles.summary: Diwali in Noida and Ghaziabad saw widespread flouting of SC firecracker time slots, with bursting till sunrise; RWAs cite weak enforcement and open sales.
articles.body: Noida: Notices were put up in the societies, advisories went out on the society WhatsApp groups and security guards were asked to intervene. But none of it could keep the crackers away. They were set off well beyond the Supreme Court-permitted slots on Nov 7 and 8 in Noida and Ghaziabad, with bursting reported past midnight and until sunrise in some areas despite repeated advisories. The court allowed crackers only from 6am to 7am and from 8pm to 10pm.The violations pointed to a wider lack of discipline and accountability. Roadside cracker sales continued openly up to society gates in several Noida sectors. In Sector 150, firecrackers were burst well past 1 am. In a Greater Noida society, youths filming reels set off crackers past 2 am. In Sector 36, a palm tree in the D block park was burnt after children burst crackers under it.Ghaziabad localities, including Indirapuram, Vaishali, Vasundhara and Shalimar Garden, also saw widespread violations. The residents’ associations said they had no authority beyond issuing advisories and arranging security interventions. They also said even police failed to enforce the deadlines.Sector 19 RWA president RC Gupta said, “Supreme Court had acknowledged that stringent restrictions without scientific backing often lead to widespread violations and that is exactly what happened over the past two days. Police and the administration should have focused on public awareness and discouraged people from bursting crackers.”Surojit Dasgupta, general secretary of the Noida Federation of Apartment Owners Association, said, “Despite our efforts through advisories and security measures, we are not enforcement agencies and lack the authority to control determined violators. The police must take responsibility for upholding the judicial directives.”Residents claimed that there was hardly any police patrolling on the internal roads during the Diwali weekend. The cops were present with PCR vans at several intersections and were answering residents’ complaints from various sectors.The violations were rampant in Greater Noida West too. A resident of Amrapali Centurian Terrace Park in Greater Noida West said their AOA asked residents to wrap up bursting crackers by 11 pm, but the sound of skyshots going off continued till sunrise.Gupta added, “It was somehow very difficult for the AOA to manage young residents. Some of them were so determined to get the perfect shot for their reels that they kept on bursting crackers. So, we had increased security measures with guards who politely asked them to slow down and celebrate responsibly.”Kapil Mehra, former AOA vice president of Amrapali Zodiac Sector 120, pointed out the broader issues at play: “It’s not just about timing; there’s a complete lack of discipline. AOAs cannot monitor every individual or turn residential complexes into enforcement zones. The administration must step up.”Environmental activist Abhisht Kusum Gupta said crackers in Sector 137 continued well past midnight, with some bursting until 3-4 am. Much of the bursting involved loud, non-green crackers, including those set off on roads, in parks and in neighbouring societies, he said.The problem extended beyond bursting timings. Nikhil Singhal, president of Noida Highrise Federation, flagged the open sale of crackers near residential gates in Sector 119, alleging that basic safety measures were missing. Avinash Arun, AOA secretary of RG Residency, Sector 120, said unrestricted sales made it easier for people to buy and burst crackers.In Ghaziabad, however, associations pointed to another complication: religious sentiments. With Diwali closely tied to faith and tradition, objections to late-night bursting were often perceived as interference in celebrations, making it difficult for RWAs and AOAs to intervene. “In the absence of adequate powers and administrative support, RWAs and AOAs feel largely helpless,” said Avneesh Kumar Jha, AOA president of Angel Mercury, Ahinsa Khand 2, Indirapuram, who is also secretary of the Federation of AOAs, Ghaziabad.Sudershan Awasth, general secretary of the Indirapuram Welfare Association, said crackers began bursting as early as 4 am, with pollution levels becoming “out of control”.Residents across both cities said the consequences went beyond noise and air pollution. Late-night explosions disturbed elderly people and children, while the risk of fire in high-rise complexes remained a serious concern.
